papers.title: Cautious Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient Methods
papers.abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are indispensable tools for modeling complex phenomena in physics and engineering. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional numerical solvers by directly incorporating physical constraints into neural network loss functions. Despite their advantages, PINN training requires multi-objective optimization, which often leads to significant gradient conflicts among boundary, initial, and residual loss terms. The Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient (ConFIG) method addresses these conflicts; however, integrating ConFIG with adaptive optimizers such as Adam introduces a critical vulnerability: the conflict-free direction generated by ConFIG is further processed by the optimizer, and the resulting weight update may no longer be conflict-free with respect to the task gradients. To address this issue, Cautious ConFIG is proposed as a concise three-line extension to the ConFIG algorithm that empirically restores the conflict-freeness guarantee prior to the weight update. The method is evaluated on three PINN benchmarks: the 1D Viscous Burgers' equation, the 1D Nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation, and the 2D Kovasznay flow. Experimental results demonstrate consistent performance improvements over the standard ConFIG baseline. Additionally, the stabilizing effect of cautious masking and its reaction to conflict severity, task number, and optimizer lag are investigated using a simple toy system.

papers.intro:
Partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely applied in physics Sommerfeld (1949), chemistry Jamwal et al. (2025), engineering Ames (1965), and finance Duffy (2013) to model complex phenomena that evolve over space and time. These equations implicitly define a function of several variables, and solving a PDE with given initial and boundary conditions involves determining this function. Traditionally, PDEs and their initial boundary value (IBV) problems are solved using numerical methods that discretize the domain into a finite set of subregions. The solution function is then represented as a set of values corresponding to these subregions. For example, the PDE can be reformulated as a time-stepping rule by approximating partial derivatives with finite differences. Discretization may introduce artifacts, particularly for complex geometries, and the number of subregions can increase exponentially with the number of dimensions, a phenomenon known as the curse of dimensionality Bellman (2015). Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) Raissi et al. (2019) have gained significant attention in recent years by directly parameterizing the solution function with a neural network. This approach mitigates discretization errors and alleviates the curse of dimensionality. As a mesh-free method, it is well-suited for complex geometries. Furthermore, formulating IBV problems as neural network training enables the utilization of recent advances in deep learning architectures and optimization techniques. However, PINNs also present limitations, as deep learning methods are less well-understood regarding error analysis and generalization compared to classical numerical approaches. While numerical methods reliably yield solutions when conditions such as the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy criterion Courant et al. (1952) are satisfied, training a neural network in a high-dimensional loss landscape can be unpredictable. One notable challenge in PINN training is gradient interference. Each IBV condition is formulated as a separate loss function, and the resulting gradients can interact adversely, severely hindering convergence. The ConFIG method Liu et al. (2025) was developed to address the gradient interference problem by computing an update direction that is conflict-free with respect to all task gradients. However, the ConFIG direction typically serves as an input to another optimizer, such as Adam Kingma and Ba (2014), and the resulting update direction may not remain conflict-free with respect to the task gradients. Consequently, the conflict-freeness property is often lost before the weight update is applied. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce Cautious ConFIG, a simple three-line extension compatible with any ConFIG-optimizer combination. It incurs negligible computational overhead, is easily parallelizable on the GPU, and effectively restores ConFIG’s mathematical properties. • We evaluate Cautious ConFIG on three challenging PINN benchmarks: the 1D viscous Burgers equation, the 1D nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the 2D Kovasznay flow, observing substantial performance improvements over the baseline (19% to 28% relative improvement). • We analyze the effectiveness of Cautious ConFIG by monitoring key metrics during PINN training and present a computational model demonstrating that Cautious ConFIG produces update directions that align more closely with task gradients under conditions of severe conflict, numerous tasks, and significant optimizer lag.

papers.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly
papers.abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.

LLM agents can now run for multiple hours on a single task autonomously. For example, a single run of PostTrainBench (Rank et al., 2026) or ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026) produces on average several hundreds of thousands of tokens, more than many LLMs’ context windows. Widely used agent scaffolds like Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenHands, and OpenCode mostly handle this with some form of summarization: when the context is near the limit, the scaffold asks a model to summarize the work so far, discards the current context, and continues from the summary (Cassano and Rush, 2026; Anthropic, 2026a; Smith, 2025; OpenCode contributors, 2026). This process is called context compaction.

This process is called context compaction.

Most compaction methods are lossy by design. If the summary removes something, the agent can then lose task constraints, certain instructions, or the chain of thought behind previous decisions. This raises two questions: can the agent still solve the task, and does it still respect the rules it was given? Previous works have shown that constraints specified by the user often do not survive compaction (Wang et al., 2026). Other work compares compaction with other context management methods on downstream accuracy, but on long context question answering or web search, where the long input is given upfront (Zhang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). However, none of these studies measure the downstream effect of compaction on realistic long horizon agentic tasks with frontier models, where the context is generated by the agent itself.

papers.title: Aligning Large Language Models with Human Feedback: Mathematical Foundations and Algorithm Design
papers.abstract: This article provides an introduction to the mathematical foundations and algorithmic frameworks used to align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intentions, preferences, and values. We discuss standard alignment techniques, such as fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO). We also explore the theoretical underpinnings of learning from human preferences, drawing connections to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and discrete choice models. We present state-of-the-art algorithms in a tutorial style, discuss their advantages and limitations, and offer insights into practical implementation. Our exposition is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners, providing both a foundational understanding of alignment methodologies and a framework for developing more robust and scalable alignment techniques.

Background. As large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm, it is clear that generative AI systems will soon become ubiquitous in our lives. LLMs have been applied beyond chatbots and personal assistants to tackle complex challenges, including video gaming [8] and autonomous control [7]. After the successful introduction and demonstrated efficacy of alignment training in LLMs [5, 38], the concept of alignment has been playing an increasingly important role in the design and training of AI systems. Loosely speaking, alignment refers to the performance guarantee that the AI system will generate outcomes that are intended or preferred by the human user without undesirable side effects or behaviors such as deception or manipulation.

Background. As large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm, it is clear that generative AI systems will soon become ubiquitous in our lives. LLMs have been applied beyond chatbots and personal assistants to tackle complex challenges, including video gaming [8] and autonomous control [7]. After the successful introduction and demonstrated efficacy of alignment training in LLMs [5, 38], the concept of alignment has been playing an increasingly important role in the design and training of AI systems. Loosely speaking, alignment refers to the performance guarantee that the AI system will generate outcomes that are intended or preferred by the human user without undesirable side effects or behaviors such as deception or manipulation.

More technically, the LLM alignment problem involves fine-tuning or adjusting a base model that was originally trained on extensive, diverse datasets. While such a base model is trained to learn core behaviors and general knowledge, it often falls short when applied to specific tasks or to meeting the nuanced preferences of a human user. To better align the model, additional feedback is gathered from human experts who evaluate and/or rank the model’s performance within a specific task context. As demonstrated in [38, 19], reinforcement learning (RL) holds significant promise for LLM alignment by leveraging additional feedback to enhance their performance. This feedback embodies expert judgments regarding both the accuracy of the model’s responses and any particular preferences they may have. The goal is to refine the model to better meet these specific requirements, ultimately enhancing its task relevance and user satisfaction. Generally, it is observed that after the alignment process, LLMs can follow human instructions well, and can avoid providing toxic and non-preferable responses. Please refer to Fig. 1 as an illustration of the alignment process.

Despite extensive study of the alignment problem in recent literature, this research area remains young, and it is still evolving rapidly with many unresolved theoretical challenges. A primary contribution of this article is to introduce the signal processing community to the fundamentals of alignment, highlight state-of-the-art algorithms and approaches, and clarify the intersection

between alignment methodologies and various techniques relevant to signal processing (SP). We believe that our article will foster interdisciplinary contributions and expand the role of SP in LLM alignment research. By understanding the alignment problem, SP researchers can leverage their expertise in mathematical modeling, noise handling, inverse problem-solving, and optimization to address a number of key challenges. For instance, similar to reconstructing signals from observed data in SP, many alignment approaches involve solving inverse problems, such as learning the human preference models from the data. Therefore, we expect that introducing the alignment to SP professionals can foster innovation in AI safety, inspire novel techniques, and accelerate the development of robust, generalizable alignment frameworks that can be applied across diverse applications.

papers.title: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference
papers.abstract: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

papers.intro:
Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations (Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009; Deng et al., 2013; Gunn & Anderson, 2015). Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays (Liu et al., 2019; Kuutti et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2025; Bodmer et al., 2026), while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016; Shi et al., 2016). These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety (Shin & Cui, 1995; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004; Ma et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2023; Nan et al., 2026).

papers.title: Phronix: The Capability-Centric Learning Paradigm for Agents
papers.abstract: Scientific computing increasingly relies on large language model-based agents for performance engineering tasks such as instrumentation, analysis, and workflow porting. However, agent effectiveness depends heavily on the surrounding harness, which typically relies on manually written skills and curated memory. This limits autonomous learning, forcing agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions rather than retain and reuse knowledge from prior executions. We introduce Phronix, a capability-centric learning paradigm that enables agentic harnesses to acquire, validate, and refine reusable capabilities from their own executions. Phronix operates through a predictor-validator-corrector loop: MCP tools and associated skills propose solutions, tool executions validate them, and observed outcomes refine the stored capabilities. It distills every observed interaction into a capability store and researches a failing task rather than abandoning it. First, such learned capabilities solve a recurring task on the first attempt in 93-95% of cases across every model, significantly reducing solution non-determinism and improving reliability. Second, Phronix turns an agent's own execution into 7.6-30.8 durable capabilities per task without user instruction, and creation falls below two once the needed capability exists. Third, warm-start runs consume only 0.38-0.40 million tokens per task, which is three to four times less than a single baseline attempt, while a cold-start costs no more than the baseline. On the 1000 Genome Pegasus workflow, instrumenting a production application for I/O performance analysis, Phronix passes all 11 correctness checks against six for the baseline harness, and also lifts the task solving rates of two cheaper models from 29% and 27% of SWE-bench tasks solved to 91% and 87%, respectively, matching the performance of the most expensive evaluated model.

papers.intro:
Scientific computing has begun to delegate its routine engineering to LLM (LLM) agents, which auto-tune HPC code on production supercomputers [13], diagnose parallel I/O performance [11], and work on the repositories and pipelines behind published results [10, 5]. The work delegated there is repetitive rather than novel, such as instrumenting an application, characterizing where a run spends its time, and repeating that for the next application, input scale, and system. An agent, however, is more than a model which operates withing a harness [34], where the LLM proposes each step and observes its result [35], tools exposed through interfaces such as the MCP (MCP) [29, 3] let it touch the world, skills accumulate how a class of task is done [33, 1], memory carries what earlier sessions learned past the context window [24], and the harness orchestrates them into the loop the agent runs. An agent that is good at such a task once should be good at it every time, and it is the harness, not the model, that determines whether it is, because the harness governs how much human steering a task requires and how many tokens and retries it consumes. Improving agent effectiveness is consequently as much a harness problem as it is a model problem.

Traditionally, LLM were accessed through web chat interfaces such as Open WebUI [20], ChatGPT [21], and Claude [2], which wrap a model in a conversation backed by a fixed set of tools [19, 29, 27]. As these interfaces matured, developers built more complex and capable command-line harnesses such as Codex [22] and OpenCode [23], which let users plug in different skills and agents for each task. State-of-the-art harnesses such as Claude Code [1] and Stakpak [31] add memory that persists across sessions, together with rulebooks that curate the standard operating procedure for a class of task. Along this timeline, each harness has become more adaptable than the last, and that adaptation is increasingly carried by skills and memory rather than by the interface itself [33, 30, 25, 24]. All of them are driven primarily by human, who writes the skill or rulebook that a complex task needs before it is assigned.

Despite support for skills and persistent memory, existing harnesses often rely on users to decide what knowledge to retain and reuse, limiting their ability to learn autonomously from completed tasks. For an agent to learn from its own work instead, the harness must overcome three challenges that each keep the user in the learning loop. First, solution non-determinism prevents an agent from reproducing a solution it has already found, because the skills and models of the harness keep changing how they solve the same problem, so a task solved once may be solved differently or not at all when it recurs. Second, manual tracking requires users to identify and preserve useful information from agent executions, so the experience a task produced is lost before it can be reused. Third, manual learning leaves the conversion of that experience into reusable knowledge to a user who must ask for a skill by name, so an agent that repeats a task never becomes better at it. These challenges are particularly significant in scientific computing, where the same instrumentation, performance analysis, and workflow porting recur across applications and systems. Addressing them requires a learning paradigm in which agents organically build, correct, and learn capabilities without waiting for a user to do so on their behalf.

We present Phronix, a learning paradigm that makes building capabilities the first-class citizen of the harness and runs every one of them as a predictor–validator–corrector loop, where a capability generates an artifact, tool-based validation deterministically rules on its correctness, and the findings of that ruling correct the capability for future use rather than working around it. Phronix addresses the three challenges through complementary mechanisms. First, deterministic but intelligent capabilities combine an MCP tool for reproducible execution with a skill that provides contextual judgment and handles corner cases, reducing solution non-determinism. Second, automatic tracking and knowledge creation, captures the inputs, execution steps, and outputs of harness–model interactions and distills them into reusable knowledge without user intervention. papers.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
papers.abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.

Recent test-time training (TTT) frameworks, such as TTT-Discover [36] and ThetaEvolve [33], provide a promising solution to this challenge by combining iterative search with test-time reinforcement learning (RL) [28, 8]. Specifically, an LLM generates candidate solutions and receives evaluation feedback. These evaluated attempts provide training data for RL, which internalizes search experience in model weights to guide subsequent generation. Their results demonstrate that TTT is a powerful test-time adaptation method on challenging scientific discovery tasks, enabling smaller open-weight models to outperform inference-only systems based on frontier models, such as AlphaEvolve [22]. However, TTT requires online model weight adaptation during the whole discovery process, which is usually computationally expensive and time-consuming (see Table 3). This motivates us to explore: under the same discovery framework, is there a more efficient test-time adaptation method that can achieve comparable or even better performance than test-time training?

papers.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
papers.abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
papers.intro:
Modern agents can often correct their mistakes and complete the task at hand. Yet, this recovery is ephemeral: In a new session, the agent is just as likely to repeat the same mistake (Rabanser et al., 2026; Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026). As agents tackle longer-horizon workflows, each additional step introduces another opportunity for error. Even frontier agents make mistakes across tool use, coding, and general assistant tasks (Yuan et al., 2026; Bandi et al., 2026). Repeatedly correcting the same mistakes is costly, leads to inconsistent performance, and leaves the potential for continuous improvement unrealized. Our goal is not just to fix an agent’s mistake in the current session, but to learn persistent lessons to avoid repeating the mistake in the future.

Existing approaches encapsulate lessons either in context or in model weights, but enable only part of the desired behavior. Context-based methods, e.g., demonstrations, prompt optimization, reflection, hard-coded skill files, and persistent agent harnesses, can change behavior quickly during deployment (Shinn et al., 2023; Majumder et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024). They enable agents to accumulate experience without access to model parameters, but their lessons remain external: They must be retrieved when relevant, compete for limited context, and may not reliably influence behavior on related future tasks.

Conversely, parameter-based methods, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, can produce more persistent behavioral change, but typically require separate training processes, substantial data and optimization, and careful management of interference to reduce the risk of catastrophic forgetting (Luo et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024; Ven et al., 2025). What is missing is a continuous mechanism to fix mistakes in the current session and avoid repeating mistakes in future sessions, without impacting existing capabilities.

To address this gap, we introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from their mistakes. After a failed execution, the agent examines its trajectory to extract a lesson and then distills the lesson into a lightweight Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) repair adapter. Self-Direction turns feedback about a mistake from the environment or a user into a LoRA lesson that can be employed immediately to retry the current task and retained for future use. Self-Direction uses a router to determine if an existing lesson is relevant to the current task based on the similarity between the current task description and descriptions of previously seen tasks, enabling reuse of lessons on future tasks. Each lesson is encoded in a separate adapter while the base model and previously learned adapters remain frozen, preventing new training from overwriting existing parameters. Furthermore, each lesson requires only a modest amount of memory (e.g., ∼85\sim 85 MB for Qwen3.6-27B), allowing the library of lessons to grow with the agent’s experience. An overview of Self-Direction is presented in Fig. 3.

papers.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
papers.abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.
papers.intro:
Many theoretical papers in statistics, machine learning, operations research and mathematics rest on long technical proofs with many tedious details. Even after several rounds of proofreading, an author can easily overlook a detail that seems unimportant, such as a boundary case, a missing regularity condition, or a step that needs an assumption the paper never states. Most of the time, such gaps have no effect on the main conclusions.

Many theoretical papers in statistics, machine learning, operations research and mathematics rest on long technical proofs with many tedious details. Even after several rounds of proofreading, an author can easily overlook a detail that seems unimportant, such as a boundary case, a missing regularity condition, or a step that needs an assumption the paper never states. Most of the time, such gaps have no effect on the main conclusions.

A proof assistant such as Lean [1], with its mathematical library Mathlib [2], accepts a proof only when every step follows from the definitions and earlier results, so no gap can pass unnoticed. Formalizing a paper in Lean is therefore a reliable way for authors to find and close the gaps in their own proofs, and the result is a paper whose mathematics is Lean-verified. Formalizing a research paper by hand, however, can take weeks of work from someone fluent in both the paper’s field and Lean. Recent agentic systems formalize informal mathematics automatically, but a research paper raises two problems that a machine cannot settle alone. First, natural language is ambiguous. A statement can admit several readings, and a formalization of the wrong one proves something the author never meant. Second, when a statement turns out to be false, there are usually many ways to fix it. The repair that changes the least in logic may still miss what the author intends, for example by giving up the part of the result the author cares about most. Both problems depend on the author’s intent, so the author has to take part in the process. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based pipeline that helps authors improve their own papers. PaperFormalizer points the author to each gap in the proofs, recommends how to close it, and produces a Lean-verified version of the paper, while the author keeps every decision about what the paper claims.

The pipeline has two stages, natural language review and autoformalization (Figure 1). In the first stage, one agent transcribes the TeX source into a dependency graph whose nodes are the statements of the paper. A second agent then checks each node closely for correctness and ambiguity and proposes repairs for the problems it finds. Whenever the agent is unsure what a statement is meant to say, it stops and asks the author, in natural language and TeX symbols, and the author decides on every repair that would weaken a main result. Once the paper passes this stage, the pipeline formalizes each statement in Lean automatically. The final output is a revised paper and a report of what was changed, together with the Lean code. We used PaperFormalizer on three of our own papers. Five of the seven results in one paper and 15 of the 29 results in another needed some revision, and for each of them the pipeline proposed a repair that largely preserve the statement of the main results in the paper. papers.title: Rethinking Multi-View Fusion for Urban Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Urban region representation learning encodes heterogeneous urban signals, such as mobility flows, points of interest, and land-use patterns, into unified embeddings for downstream tasks, including check-in prediction, crime forecasting, and service demand estimation. Existing approaches rely on globally shared fusion and joint optimization, implicitly assuming uniform modality importance and naturally balanced multi-objective training. However, urban data is inherently heterogeneous. Our empirical analysis reveals two structural issues: (i) modality utility varies markedly across regions, causing static fusion to overemphasize signals from certain modalities; and (ii) heterogeneous objectives exhibit persistent gradient imbalance, causing representational bias and unstable training. We present PRISM, a self-adjusting framework for adaptive multi-view learning. PRISM adapts sparse MoE routing to learn region-specific view allocations, while a PID (Proportional Integral Derivative)-inspired regulation mechanism mitigates gradient conflicts during optimization. Experiments on three large-scale urban datasets show that PRISM achieves competitive performance compared with strong multi-view baselines, while providing more stable optimization behavior and more balanced region representations.

Cities are increasingly instrumented with sensing and digital infrastructures that continuously generate heterogeneous data from mobility networks, land-use registries, transportation systems, and socio-economic activities (Xu et al., 2025a). This data provides unprecedented opportunities for understanding urban dynamics. Yet, heterogeneity in terms of structure, granularity, noise ratio, and spatial coverage poses fundamental data integration and computational modeling challenges.

Cities are increasingly instrumented with sensing and digital infrastructures that continuously generate heterogeneous data from mobility networks, land-use registries, transportation systems, and socio-economic activities (Xu et al., 2025a). This data provides unprecedented opportunities for understanding urban dynamics. Yet, heterogeneity in terms of structure, granularity, noise ratio, and spatial coverage poses fundamental data integration and computational modeling challenges.

Urban region representation learning has emerged as a principled abstraction for addressing these challenges (Duan et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2027). Transforming diverse urban signals into compact embeddings enables computational models that capture latent spatial functionality and inter-region relationships in a unified vector form. These embeddings serve as reusable, transferable representations that support a wide range of analytical tasks, including check-in prediction (Liang and Zhang, 2023; Gong et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025), crime forecasting (Butt et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023), traffic modeling (Zhang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2021b; Yang et al., 2022a; Yang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2027; Yang et al., 2021a; Yang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2022b; Wei et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b; Yang and Yang, 2020), and service demand estimation (Sun et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025a).

Structured multi-view fusion. Existing approaches treat each urban modality—such as mobility flow graphs, POI distributions, or land-use maps—as an independent structured signal that is encoded using graph or attribute-based models. Representative methods (e.g., MGFN (Wu et al., 2022), HAFusion (Sun et al., 2024), CGAP (Xu and Zhou, 2024)) jointly learn representations from multiple modalities and fuse them by means of concatenation, attention, or weighted aggregation. More recent studies extend this paradigm to cross-modal settings by incorporating additional sources such as street-view images (e.g., FlexiReg (Sun et al., 2025a)). While being architecturally diverse, these methods adopt a shared abstraction: heterogeneous views are integrated via globally shared fusion mechanisms under deterministic parameterization.

Multi-objective optimization in multi-view learning. Multi-view urban representation learning typically introduces modality-specific objectives that guide the shared embedding towards distinct structural or semantic properties. These objectives are then jointly optimized within a unified parameter space without explicit coordination. Although general multi-task strategies (e.g., gradient normalization or projection) have been explored in other domains, they assume task symmetry and do not account for the spatially heterogeneous and modality-dependent dynamics intrinsic to urban data.

Motivating example. To evaluate these assumptions, we analyze on three city-scale datasets (see Figure 1). Figure 1a highlights task-dependent differences in modality utility: mobility signals are most informative for crime prediction, whereas land-use and POI features are more useful for service call prediction, suggesting differing underlying spatial dynamics. Notably, as highlighted by the red dashed oval, POI and land-use features contribute negligibly to the SF Crime task. This pronounced heterogeneity challenges the assumption of globally uniform fusion across modalities. Figure 1b further reveals a systematic optimization imbalance under conventional joint training (e.g., the red dashed oval). Gradients associated with different modality-specific objectives exhibit persistent magnitude disparities, allowing dominant modalities to steer the shared embedding space while suppressing weaker yet informative signals. Such imbalance induces representational bias and ultimately degrades cross-region generalization.

Following this analysis, we identify two coupled research challenges that remain unresolved in urban region representation learning:

Challenge 1 (C1): Spatially adaptive view integration. The predictive utility of each modality is inherently region-dependent, and yet existing fusion mechanisms assign contributions through globally shared parameters. This mismatch between local data characteristics and global fusion strategies incurs representational bias—commercial regions may be well-served while residential regions may be systematically under-represented. The challenge is to enable region-aware, adaptive modality selection that aligns representation capacity with spatial heterogeneity, without requiring region-specific supervision.

Challenge 2 (C2): Coordinated optimization under heterogeneous objectives. When multiple modality-specific objectives with different gradient scales, noise levels, and convergence rates are jointly optimized in a shared embedding space, objectives associated with certain modalities may contribute disproportionately large or more stable gradients, causing them to dominate the optimization process and suppress weaker modality signals, which in turn leads to imbalanced representations and unstable training. papers.title: Towards Adversarially Robust Multigraph Neural Networks for Financial Crime Analysis
papers.abstract: Financial transaction networks are naturally represented as multigraphs, where repeated transactions between the same pair of accounts are modeled as distinct edges. Recently proposed multigraph neural network architectures leverage this structure explicitly to achieve a strong performance on anti-money laundering (AML) tasks. However, their robustness to adversaries that manipulate transaction structures to evade detection remains largely unexplored. We present the first scalable framework for structural attacks and adversarial training of multigraph neural networks using node-edge incidence matrices, adapting projected gradient descent and projected randomized block coordinate descent methods to optimize structural perturbations over such matrices. We further introduce a cycle-based regularizer that penalizes changes in the global counts of directed 2- and 3-cycles, providing a structural measure of attack plausibility. Experiments on synthetic pattern-detection and realistic AML datasets show that our learned attacks substantially outperform non-learnable perturbation baselines in reducing detection performance (PR-AUC), while adversarial training consistently improves robustness against these attacks. These results demonstrate that multigraph neural networks are vulnerable to learned structural attacks and that adversarial training provides an effective defense. Our code is available at https://github.com/denheijmans/robust_multignn.
papers.intro:
Money laundering involves transferring proceeds of crime through the financial system, with an estimated 2–5% of global GDP laundered each year [1]. Illegal transfers are hidden within billions of transactions flowing between legitimate accounts every day. Detecting them increasingly relies on automated analysis of the transaction networks formed by those payments. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as the leading tool for this task [2, 3, 4, 5, 6], reaching high detection accuracy in structural pattern analysis and transaction classification.

Illegal transfers are hidden within billions of transactions flowing between legitimate accounts every day. Detecting them increasingly relies on automated analysis of the transaction networks formed by those payments. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as the leading tool for this task [2, 3, 4, 5, 6], reaching high detection accuracy in structural pattern analysis and transaction classification.

Furthermore, financial crime is often structured to evade detection [7]. Breaking large transfers into smaller ones, routing funds through intermediary accounts, and timing transactions to fall below reporting thresholds are documented evasion tactics that reshape the financial transaction graph. This threat raises a concrete question: can an adversary manipulate the structure of a transaction network by adding or removing transactions to cause a graph neural network to miss criminal activity?

Breaking large transfers into smaller ones, routing funds through intermediary accounts, and timing transactions to fall below reporting thresholds are documented evasion tactics that reshape the financial transaction graph. This threat raises a concrete question: can an adversary manipulate the structure of a transaction network by adding or removing transactions to cause a graph neural network to miss criminal activity?

Importantly, financial transaction networks are naturally modeled as multigraphs, where the same pair of accounts may exchange multiple payments over time and each transaction has its own attributes, such as amount and timestamp. These attributes are essential for capturing financial crime patterns in transaction graphs. papers.title: Every Weight Is a Path of Shared Discrete Decisions
papers.abstract: We introduce TWIG (Tree-structured Weights with Inherited Gates), a representation in which every weight of a neural network is the end of a path of small discrete decisions: a sign, a shift by a power of two, a zero gate, an index into a shared table. Weights that belong together share the upper part of their paths, and each decision is inherited by every weight below it, so it is stored once and applied once. This simple change has three consequences. Any trained network can be written as a TWIG, and when the decisions are powers of two its weight layers become circuits made almost entirely of wires and adders, suited to chips whose weights are fixed at fabrication. Pruning, quantization, low-rank factorization, codebooks and weight sharing become edits of one object, so a single optimizer can choose among all of them for a whole network. And choosing the decisions is the ground-state problem of a higher-order Boltzmann machine whose interactions follow the paths of the tree, the problem class that annealers and quantum optimizers are built to solve. Today these questions are handled apart: each compression method brings its own format and solver, a circuit with fixed weights needs a dedicated constant multiplier for every weight, and discrete solvers reach only narrow subproblems such as rounding. Weight formats have long been moving toward shared decisions, through group scales, shared exponents, microexponents and sparse weights; TWIG takes this trend to its end, and every common format is a shallow TWIG at no extra cost. On five weight matrices of a large language model, a flat tree whose signed power-of-two terms are chosen per weight for circuit cost, with no group scales, needs 9--15\% fewer additions than GPTQ at equal layer error at 3- and 4-bit accuracy on typical matrices, and 20--55\% fewer on matrices with strong outliers.

Modern neural networks are trained in the continuum. Gradient descent needs a smooth landscape to follow, so weights are modelled as real numbers and learning is described as motion through a high-dimensional real space; much of what we understand about optimization and generalization rests on this view. Deployment, however, takes place in a discrete world. On digital hardware, every weight is a finite bit pattern drawn from a fixed format, every product is computed by a circuit of logic gates, and every byte has to be moved through a memory hierarchy. The passage from the continuous model that was learned to the discrete object that is executed is therefore unavoidable, and it has grown into a research field of its own.

That field has grown in pieces. Pruning removes weights, quantization restricts them to finite grids, low-rank factorization replaces matrices by products of thinner ones, codebook methods map blocks of weights to entries of a shared table, and weight sharing reuses parameters across layers. Each family brings its own storage format, its own solver and often its own kernel, and combining them (four bits in one layer, half of the weights pruned in another, a low-rank correction in a third) remains largely a matter of manual design, without a common yardstick. Two further questions sit almost entirely outside this picture. The first is the cost of computing with the weights rather than storing them: in digital logic a multiplier is considerably larger and more energy-hungry than an adder [30], and in circuits whose weights are fixed at fabrication, such as printed classifiers [57] or chips that hardwire an entire language model [71], every weight calls for a constant multiplier of its own. The second is the reach of discrete optimization: choosing discrete weights is a combinatorial problem, yet annealers, samplers and quantum optimizers, which are built for exactly such problems, have so far been applied only to narrow parts of it, such as the rounding of a single layer [59]. What is missing, we argue, is a representation of weights that is discrete by construction, that makes the structure shared by weights explicit, and that exposes the cost of applying them.

papers.title: Not All Retained Clients Are Equal: Client Selection for Federated Unlearning
papers.abstract: Federated unlearning (FU) aims to remove a designated target client's influence from a trained model without the prohibitive cost of retraining from scratch. Existing methods largely treat unlearning as a post-hoc, stateless operation, overlooking that client influence is path-dependent: contributions made during training, particularly during critical learning periods (CLPs), can have disproportionate and persistent effects. Moreover, knowledge overlap and intermittent client availability make relying on all retained clients inefficient and impractical. We introduce PDF, a path-dependent client-selection framework based on the insight that retained clients are not equally valuable for unlearning. During training, PDF maintains lightweight, target-agnostic, CLP-weighted histories summarizing each client's accumulated update direction and global-model alignment. Upon an unlearning request, these histories identify and rank retained clients that are globally informative yet weakly coupled to the target, enabling retraining-based unlearning with only the top-$k$ clients over a small number of rounds. Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under IID and non-IID settings show that PDF achieves effective forgetting and strong retained utility with substantially fewer retained clients. In particular, PDF achieves $0\%$ forgetting accuracy with retraining-like MIA AUC on non-IID CIFAR-10, improves retained accuracy by up to $6.91$ percentage points over the strongest competing FU baseline on CIFAR-100, and reduces communication by approximately $69\%$ and computation by $57$--$61\%$ relative to Retrain.

papers.intro:
As federated learning (FL) gains traction in privacy-sensitive and highly regulated domains (e.g., healthcare [29, 11]), deployed systems must accommodate not only privacy-preserving model training but also the post-training removal of client data influence–whether to comply with legal obligations, such as the right to be forgotten under the GDPR [26], or to mitigate impacts of contributions from corrupted, low-quality, or malicious clients. These operational and regulatory demands have given rise to federated unlearning (FU), which aims to eliminate the influence of designated target clients from a trained global model while preserving the knowledge contributed by the remaining clients.

These operational and regulatory demands have given rise to federated unlearning (FU), which aims to eliminate the influence of designated target clients from a trained global model while preserving the knowledge contributed by the remaining clients.

Existing FU methods, including retraining-based approaches [19, 39, 35] and model-manipulation approaches [32, 16, 40, 9, 22, 33], face three major limitations in addressing client-level unlearning. First, they overlook how client influence develops throughout the training stage. In FL, client participation and update directions vary across rounds; therefore, a client’s influence on the final model depends not only on whether it participates, but also on when it participates. This temporal structure is particularly important during critical learning periods (CLPs), in which client updates can have disproportionately persistent effects on the learned representations, optimization trajectory, and final model performance [1, 17, 37, 36]. Moreover, under heterogeneous data, changing participation, or adaptive optimization, critical phases may emerge beyond a fixed early-training window [13, 30]. Second, retraining-based methods incur substantial computation, communication, and storage overhead because they reconstruct or recalibrate the model using all retained clients. Their effectiveness therefore depends on continuous availability of clients after training, an assumption that may not hold in practical FL systems with intermittent or voluntary participation. Third, efficient model-manipulation methods often face a pronounced trade-off between target forgetting efficacy and retained-model utility [9, 6, 33]. Achieving stronger forgetting may excessively perturb knowledge shared with retained clients, whereas preserving utility may leave residual target influence. They may also rely on expensive server-side operations or require future unlearning targets to be anticipated during the original training stage [6, 9, 40, 32, 22].

We argue that these limitations share a common cause: existing FU methods are largely model layer-, parameter-, or protocol-centric and treat unlearning as a stateless operation, overlooking the impacts of heterogeneous influence that clients accumulate over training. We instead formulate client-level unlearning as an inherently path-dependent client-selection problem. Inspired by path dependence in economics [3], we posit that a client’s influence is shaped not only by its final contribution, but also by when that influence emerged, particularly during CLPs, and by how strongly it became coupled with other clients. Thus, effective unlearning should select retained clients according to their historical alignment with the global model and their dependence on the target clients, rather than uniformly or solely by availability. Building on this insight, we ask the following question: How can the path-dependent influence during the learning stage be exploited to improve the forgetting efficacy, retained utility, and efficiency of client-level FU?

During training, PDF maintains lightweight, target-agnostic histories that capture each client’s alignment with the global optimization trajectory, its historical update direction with other clients, and its participation during CLPs. papers.title: Towards Trustworthy AI-Enabled Emergency Medical Dispatch: Uncertainty-Aware Ambulance Travel Time Estimation
papers.abstract: Emergency medical dispatch increasingly relies on AI-enabled decision support systems when making ambulance dispatch decisions. In this process, accurate ambulance travel time estimates are essential for timely resource allocation and prehospital care. However, existing ambulance travel time estimation approaches typically produce only single point predictions. Consequently, they do not indicate how reliable an individual estimate is or how much uncertainty it carries. This limitation is particularly problematic in safety-critical emergency medical service dispatch operations, where trips with similar expected travel times may exhibit substantially different levels of uncertainty. Furthermore, real-world ambulance trip logs may contain domain-specific artefacts, such as co-located healthcare facilities and physically implausible travel speeds. These artefacts can degrade point prediction accuracy and affect the prediction task on which subsequent uncertainty estimation depends. To address these challenges, we propose an uncertainty-aware methodology for ambulance travel time estimation and evaluate it through a retrospective real-world scenario study using two years of ambulance trip data from the Sk{\aa}ne region in Sweden. The proposed methodology moves beyond average-case point predictions by generating context-adaptive prediction intervals with stable empirical coverage across the evaluated operationally important contexts. The resulting prediction intervals provide explicit information about predictive uncertainty that can support more transparent and risk-sensitive ambulance dispatch decision-making.

papers.intro:
Emergency medical dispatch is a high-stakes decision-making process that increasingly relies on AI-enabled decision support systems that combine operational data, predictive models, and human judgement. Within this public-sector service, ambulance travel time estimation is an important component of dispatch decision support, as travel time estimates provide important information on which available unit should be assigned to an incident and how quickly prehospital care may reach the patient. Even small estimation errors can lead to the assignment of an ambulance that arrives later than another available unit, which matters most for high-priority incidents where delays may have clinical consequences. Ambulance travel time estimation is challenging because travel times vary with local conditions, dispatch priority, route characteristics, and temporal context [1]. To capture this complexity, recent research has increasingly adopted data-driven machine learning approaches that can improve predictive accuracy compared with static lookup tables, fixed-speed assumptions, and generic navigation estimates [2, 3, 4].

To capture this complexity, recent research has increasingly adopted data-driven machine learning approaches that can improve predictive accuracy compared with static lookup tables, fixed-speed assumptions, and generic navigation estimates [2, 3, 4].

However, predictive accuracy alone is insufficient for safety-critical dispatch support. Most existing ambulance travel time estimation approaches provide only a single point prediction. A single point prediction provides one estimated travel time, for example, that an ambulance will arrive in 1212 minutes, without indicating the uncertainty associated with that estimate. This missing information is important in emergency medical service (EMS) decision support because predictions with similar expected travel times may differ substantially in their uncertainty. For example, consider two ambulances available for a time-critical emergency. A point prediction model estimates travel times of 1010 minutes for Ambulance A and 1111 minutes for Ambulance B, which would favour Ambulance A based on the expected travel time alone. Suppose, however, that an uncertainty-aware methodology produces an interval of ±5\pm 5 minutes for Ambulance A and ±1\pm 1 minute for Ambulance B. If an operational criterion requires arrival within 1212 minutes, Ambulance B may represent the lower-uncertainty option under that criterion. More generally, uncertainty information could support dispatchers when considering whether an individual travel time estimate is sufficiently reliable or whether additional operational information should be considered. Thus, an uncertainty-aware estimation complements the point estimate by explicitly representing the range of plausible travel times rather than providing only an expected value. As our exploratory analysis in Section 4.3 shows, travel time variability differs across temporal conditions and route frequency groups, while substantial variability remains even among trips with similar operational characteristics.

As our exploratory analysis in Section 4.3 shows, travel time variability differs across temporal conditions and route frequency groups, while substantial variability remains even among trips with similar operational characteristics.

Another important challenge concerns the operational validity of the underlying data on which predictive models should be developed. Real-world EMS datasets may contain domain-specific artefacts that distort the prediction task. First, operationally distinct facilities, such as co-located hospitals and on-campus clinics, may be geocoded to identical coordinates, creating ambiguity in origin–destination representations. Second, a small subset of trips may have implied average speeds outside physically plausible ranges for ground ambulance transport. Extremely low speeds may indicate idle or waiting time included in the recorded trip duration, whereas implausibly low or high speeds may also result from GPS inaccuracies or timestamp inconsistencies. For example, departure or arrival events may be manually registered before or after the corresponding operational event, making the recorded trip duration too long or too short. We therefore define two curation criteria a priori from domain knowledge: removing trips between facilities that share the same coordinates and removing trips with implausible average speeds. Applying these criteria before model development provides a stronger basis for point prediction and subsequent uncertainty estimation.

In this paper, we focus on three limitations that remain insufficiently addressed in ambulance travel time estimation research: (i) deterministic predictions, which do not quantify the uncertainty associated with individual travel time estimates; (ii) operational data quality, where domain-specific artefacts in historical dispatch records may distort the prediction task; and (iii) subgroup reliability, where satisfactory aggregate calibration may conceal differences in empirical coverage across operationally relevant contexts. To address these limitations, we propose an uncertainty-aware methodology for ambulance travel time estimation and evaluate it through a retrospective real-world scenario study using two years of ambulance trip data from the Skåne region in Sweden. The proposed methodology first applies domain-informed data curation to establish an operationally valid prediction task. The resulting data are then prepared for model development, and a point prediction model is trained to estimate ambulance travel time. Conformal calibration is subsequently used to generate prediction intervals that quantify predictive uncertainty. Under the exchangeability assumption, the conformal methods provide finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. By complementing point predictions with calibrated prediction intervals and evaluating their empirical coverage across operationally relevant contexts, the proposed methodology provides a basis for assessing predictive reliability beyond conventional point prediction accuracy alone.

papers.title: Beyond Heuristics and Commercial Navigation: An AI-Augmented Decision-Support for Ambulance Travel Time Estimation
papers.abstract: Accurate ambulance travel time estimation is critical for emergency medical dispatch, yet existing decision-support practices often rely on static lookup tables or simplified assumptions regarding how ambulance travel time differs from ordinary passenger-car travel. For instance, they assume ambulances simply travel a fixed percentage (e.g., 5%) faster than ordinary passenger cars. However, such assumptions are rarely validated using real ambulance operational data and may fail to capture the effects of trip priority, temporal context, and origin-destination. We address these limitations using historical ambulance trips from the Sk{\aa}ne region in Sweden. Our analysis reveals that ambulance travel times vary substantially by hour, day, and trip priority, and that commercial navigation systems fail to capture emergency-specific dynamics. We contribute a machine learning system to more accurately estimate ambulance travel time. To make the system interpretable, we explored SHapley Additive exPlanations and permutation importance techniques to ensure that our system captures operationally meaningful patterns.

In emergency medical services (EMS), ambulance travel time is a critical input for dispatch decisions as it affects how quickly prehospital care can reach a patient [1]. Reliable travel time estimates can support ambulance selection, hospital routing, response planning, and resource allocation [2]. However, ambulance travel time is affected by several contextual factors, including temporal conditions, trip urgency, and local road-network characteristics [3]. If such factors are ignored, dispatch systems may produce estimates that do not reflect the actual operating context, which can be especially problematic in time-sensitive cases [4].

In emergency medical services (EMS), ambulance travel time is a critical input for dispatch decisions as it affects how quickly prehospital care can reach a patient [1]. Reliable travel time estimates can support ambulance selection, hospital routing, response planning, and resource allocation [2]. However, ambulance travel time is affected by several contextual factors, including temporal conditions, trip urgency, and local road-network characteristics [3]. If such factors are ignored, dispatch systems may produce estimates that do not reflect the actual operating context, which can be especially problematic in time-sensitive cases [4].

The EMS employs various systems to estimate ambulance travel time [5, 6, 10, 9]. However, these systems remain limited because they often rely on (a) generic navigation estimates, designed for ordinary passenger-car traffic; (b) fixed-ratio speed assumptions, assuming that ambulances travel at a constant speed or fixed percentage faster than regular vehicles; or (c) predetermined lookup tables, assigning fixed travel times between locations. Such approaches may not fully capture ambulance specific movement patterns, trip priority, temporal variation, or local operational conditions. As a result, they can produce estimates that are insufficiently responsive to the dynamic and context-dependent nature of emergency medical services. This motivates the need for a data-driven system offering more accurate ambulance travel time estimates to support dispatch decisions.

We contribute a data-driven, context-aware travel time estimation system that learns from real-world ambulance operations and provides more accurate, interpretable estimates and illustrate its use in a scenario study of a regional EMS system in Sweden. Our system is based on machine learning, and it adapts its prediction according to the operational trip context, offering a promising alternative to static lookup tables, fixed-ratio heuristics, and generic navigation estimates. The proposed system computes the travel time for the ambulance in a given context, including variables that significantly improve the accuracy of the estimation. These variables are the origin and destination of each trip, trip priority, and departure time variables (e.g., hour of the day and day of the week). To identify these variables, we conducted an exploratory data analysis. Thereafter, we trained a supervised machine learning regressor on the identified variables. To make the system more operationally trustworthy, we explored two interpretability approaches, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) [7] and permutation importance [8], to identify the contextual variables that most influence travel time estimates and to verify that the machine learning regressor has learned operationally meaningful patterns. The proposed system sets a new benchmark performance in estimating travel time, compared to a leading conventional system.

papers.title: Rewriting Scaling Laws for Synthetic Data with Compute and Data Constraints
papers.abstract: Synthetic rewrites, where a language model rewrites a natural document e.g. into a target style, are now a standard ingredient of pretraining corpora. However, critical aspects of their use remain poorly understood, such as how much compute should be spent rewriting training data and whether a model trained on rewrites can outperform the rewriter. We study these two questions by proposing a rewriting scaling law that predicts loss from model size, training tokens, the fraction of training tokens that are rewrites, and the number of epochs over the natural data, charging the compute spent generating rewrites. We fit this scaling law in two settings. In the compute-limited setting, natural data is plentiful and rewrites come from a third-party rewriter trained with more compute than our largest run. We find that the estimated optimal rewrite fraction increases with compute, from under $10\%$ at $3\times10^{18}$ FLOPs to $32\%$ at $10^{22}$ FLOPs. Our scaling forecast extrapolates $33\times$ in FLOPs to train a 22B-parameter model, whose final loss is within $1.1\%$ of our prediction. This model achieves a better BPB than its rewriter on several web domains at one-tenth the rewriter's training compute. In the data-limited setting, we assume we only have a fixed seed set of natural data and that our rewriter is a model of the same size as the target, pretrained on that seed set. Again, we find the optimal rewrite fraction increases with the compute budget. We also demonstrate that a model trained on rewrites of its own pretraining data, generated by a rewriter of the same size, beats the best run on natural data alone at every model size up to 3B. Our results show that synthetic rewriting can be studied through the scaling law lens: that optimal methodological choices are predictable and scaling does not necessarily break down beyond the rewriter's capabilities.

papers.title: Cognitively Constrained Partners for Zero-Shot Coordination in Real-Time Partitioned Control
papers.abstract: Effective human-machine teaming requires agents that coordinate with unpredictable human partners. Reinforcement learning from live human feedback or large behavioural datasets is expensive, while purely simulated training overfits to artificial conventions and fails at Zero-Shot Coordination with real people. We propose a framework for training teaming agents against Cognitively Constrained Partners: simulated partners whose diversity emerges from procedural constraints grounded in human physiological literature, specifically reaction delays and perceptual limitations, rather than from reward shaping or historical training checkpoints. In a modified Lunar Lander environment, we report preliminary evidence that these partners play more like real people than unconstrained agents do, and that agents trained against them match the strongest cross-play baselines while being the only ones whose performance does not depend on how their training partners were generated. We also describe a human-participant study designed so that its rankings can be compared directly against cross-play, testing how well that standard evaluation predicts real human-agent teaming.

papers.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
papers.abstract: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recently proposed extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We give a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error in terms of a residual component vanishing under compatibility. Next, we note that existing compatible objectives put density on velocities that are infeasible on compact manifolds. We propose an objective built from an exponential family over endpoints, with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. This manifests as a reweighting of the flow matching loss which, on constant-curvature manifolds, treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Empirically, our method recovers the correct velocity field on the test case, outperforms prior methods on high-dimensional product tori, and obtains substantial NLL improvements over prior work on two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere at moderate runtime overhead. On a large dataset of high-dimensional human poses, our method outperforms prior work according to sample-based metrics.
papers.intro:
Much of the success of modern generative modelling can be attributed to the development of transport-based models, which learn to deform a simple base distribution into the target data distribution. These include diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020) and normalizing flows (Tabak and Turner, 2013; Rezende and Mohamed, 2015; Papamakarios et al., 2021). In particular, conditional flow matching models (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023; Liu et al., 2023) are effective at generating images (Hu et al., 2024), video (Jin et al., 2025), and heterogeneous tabular data (Guzmán-Cordero et al., 2025). These models learn the transport map in terms of a time-dependent vector field and thus fall within the model class of continuous normalizing flows (Chen et al., 2018). To overcome the scalability challenges faced by other models in this category, flow matching decomposes the intractable marginal probability path into simpler conditional paths coupling the base and data distributions. The idea is to learn the marginal velocity field by regression onto many examples of the simple fields generating these conditional paths.

We characterize loss functions for flow matching in terms of their likelihood model, whether that is explicit (as in RG-VFM) or implicit (as in RFM). We delineate two properties. First, we say a loss function is compatible if its population optimum gives the true marginal flow induced by the data and coupling (section 3.2). This is a minimal correctness check for an objective to be generally useful. Second, we say it is support-aware if the corresponding likelihood puts mass only on velocities that are achievable (section 3.4). These are independent properties in the sense that RFM is compatible but not support-aware on compact manifolds, while RG-VFM is support-aware but not compatible (table 1). Our theoretical contributions are: • We derive a general compatibility condition for likelihood-based objectives, satisfied by RFM but not RG-VFM. We show this analytically on the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the flat torus 𝕋1\mathbb{T}^{1}. This general condition is most relevant in the manifold setting, but applies to any flow matching problem in which the conditional paths are nonlinear. • We show that the squared error in the local flow scales with the product of distributional fit and a residual term. The residual is zero for a compatible model, eliminating this source of error even when the likelihood model is misspecified. • We view RFM as maximizing likelihood over velocities in the tangent space under a Gaussian model of fixed covariance. This reveals how, despite being compatible, it omits global structure from its training signal. One example is compact manifolds, where the maximum flow speed is limited. Here, the RFM likelihood puts density on infeasible velocities. This motivates our proposed method, which is both compatible and support-aware. papers.title: REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Regularisation-based class-incremental learning (CIL) methods control the stability-plasticity trade-off through fixed coefficients tuned offline, independently of the continual learning objective and blind to phase-specific variations in data volume, task difficulty, and class similarity. We argue this is a fundamental mismatch and propose REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning, which treats regularisation strength selection as a sequential decision problem. At each incremental phase, a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) agent observes a compact state of current performance metrics and incoming data statistics, and outputs the distillation coefficients for that phase. To respect CIL's constraint on historical data access, the policy is trained entirely on pseudo-CIL tasks constructed from the initial phase, then deployed on the incremental sequence without further adaptation. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that REDAR reduces forgetting and improves forward transfer over fixed and heuristic baselines, and that policies trained on short pseudo-task horizons transfer effectively to longer incremental runs.
