Class-incremental learning (CIL) requires a model to absorb new categories sequentially while retaining performance on all previously seen classes, without access to the full historical dataset. This capability is essential for deployed perception systems and embodied agents that operate under non-stationary data streams. The central challenge is catastrophic forgetting: naive fine-tuning overwrites earlier representations as the network adapts to new data, exposing the fundamental stability–plasticity dilemma.

Class-incremental learning (CIL) requires a model to absorb new categories sequentially while retaining performance on all previously seen classes, without access to the full historical dataset. This capability is essential for deployed perception systems and embodied agents that operate under non-stationary data streams. The central challenge is catastrophic forgetting: naive fine-tuning overwrites earlier representations as the network adapts to new data, exposing the fundamental stability–plasticity dilemma.

Prior work addresses this from three angles: rehearsal, which interleaves stored exemplars with current training data [23, 17]; architecture-based methods, which grow or partition capacity to reduce interference [32, 19]; regularisation-based methods, which constrain updates via parameter penalties [12, 34] or knowledge distillation [15, 9, 5]. Despite this progress, one design choice has received little attention: how strongly should a model be regularised at each incremental step? Existing methods fix the regularisation coefficient across all phases, selected once via offline hyperparameter search [23, 9, 5, 6, 25]. This is a poor fit for realistic CIL scenarios, where successive phases differ in data volume, class imbalance, task difficulty, and similarity to prior classes, so the stability–plasticity trade-off shifts in ways a single global coefficient cannot track.

papers.title: A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens
papers.abstract: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a new interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al., 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable to the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens, and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features -- directions that act like leading, spatially coherent Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a ``Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical applied to both model classes. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens . We also introduce of a family of J-lenses built to emphasize different temporal scales of information processing in LLMs, which we call $\omega$-J-lenses.

papers.intro:
In a recent paper, Gurnee et al. (2026) introduced a novel interpretability technique that they claimed could identify an internal ‘workspace’ in large language models (LLMs), which had properties reminiscent of the Global Workspace (Baars, 1988; Dehaene et al., 1998). The object they primarily study is the ‘Jacobian lens’, or ‘J-lens’. This interpretability tool is designed in the spirit of other ‘lenses’ (nostalgebraist, 2020; Belrose et al., 2023), which seek to decode transformer hidden state activations into language by applying the unembedding matrix of the model to these activations (potentially after a learned affine map, as in the tuned lens). These lenses benefit interpretability by mapping hidden states to tokens, which are in the space of language and hopefully more interpretable. Decoding intermediate layers this way has shown that predictions are refined gradually across depth (nostalgebraist, 2020; Belrose et al., 2023), that multilingual models pass through an English-like latent space before producing the target language (Wendler et al., 2024), that false few-shot demonstrations derail predictions only after a critical layer (Halawi et al., 2024), and that a single hidden state already carries information about tokens several positions ahead (Pal et al., 2023). The trajectory of tuned-lens predictions across layers can also detect malicious inputs (Belrose et al., 2023).

The Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al., 2026) continues this line of work by introducing a new transfer operator onto the residual stream vector before the application of the unembedding matrix and mapping to tokens. This operator is the Jacobian of the transformer, averaged over tokens. In their paper, the motivation for the usage of the Jacobian 𝑲\bm{K} is based on standard results in calculus: A Jacobian describes how a small perturbation in the input of a function results in a change in the output. When the Jacobian is studied in an LLM, it provides directions in the residual stream that are “verbalizable” (Gurnee et al., 2026), which is to say that it identifies how perturbations change the linguistic output of the model. However, this property holds only in the local neighborhood of the point on which the Jacobian is defined, and the J-lens is defined by averaging over prompts, tokens, and future positions in the output layer. An average Jacobian has no reason to behave like any of its elements. Indeed, if the Jacobians of a system form a curved manifold, the average Jacobian can easily lie off-manifold. More generally, well-known features that describe the behavior of linear operators (e.g., singular vectors and values, which are nonlinear functions of a matrix) can deviate grossly from those of individual Jacobians under averaging (Appendix A). papers.title: RSI-Opt: Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents For Model Training
papers.abstract: Conventional neural-network training typically follows a predefined optimization recipe, motivating a LLM agent that monitors training dynamics and adjusts optimizer settings as training progresses, but a fixed agent policy does not accumulate experience across runs. We introduce RSI-Opt, a plug-and-play Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents which evolves the knowledge that guides this process: a prompt, a playbook of procedures, a library of tested optimizer code, and a decision cadence. A meta-agent rewrites this policy using evidence from earlier runs, and an archive retains evaluated policies for further evolution. Across 5 generations on three training tasks, the meta-agents develop reusable procedures and code and conduct their own CPU proxy experiments. RSI-Opt substantially improves optimizer-agent performance, with representative raw-space summary $z$-scores increasing from $+10.48$ to $+14.33$ on the evolution suite with Opus 5.5 and from $-0.36$ to $+3.11$ on held-out tasks with GPT-5.5 through cross-model policy transfer. On the Burgers PDE, it reduces mean relative $L_2$ error by approximately 2.7-fold with Opus 5.5 and 8.8-fold with GPT-6.1 over the fixed-prompt agent baseline, although PDE transfer varies across LLMs and tasks. Controlled comparisons show that the evolved policy combines reusable optimization knowledge with adaptation to each task: initial decisions capture most observed gains on seen tasks, while continued adaptation improves outcomes on unseen tasks. These findings demonstrate how procedures and executable tools accumulated across training runs can improve optimizer-agent performance and support transfer to scientific machine learning.
papers.intro:
Neural-network training usually begins with an optimizer and schedule chosen in advance. Their effectiveness can depend on the architecture, data, and training dynamics, yet selecting a new recipe often requires repeated runs and manual intervention. A coding agent offers another form of adaptation: it can inspect a training run and revise the optimizer’s program while the model trains. Concurrent work on reactive optimizers, OPAL [2], studies this within-run setting. A single LLM agent observes training dynamics and revises the update rule, learning rates, schedules, and diagnostics during an individual run. Its conversation persists within that run, but its fixed initial policy does not retain lessons for the next one. A useful optimizer change, a misleading diagnostic, or a tested implementation must be rediscovered when a new run starts.We study whether optimizer agents can improve this initial policy across runs through recursive self-improvement. RSI-Opt makes the agent’s accumulated knowledge an explicit, editable object: a prompt, a playbook of procedures and lessons, a library of optimizer and diagnostic code, and a decision cadence. An outer meta-agent reads evidence from earlier runs, modifies a parent policy, and evaluates the child on a training suite. An archive supports continued exploration and inheritance, following the archive-based approach of the Darwin Gödel Machine [35]. The underlying LLM weights, meta-agent instructions, and evaluator remain fixed; the policy used to improve optimizers is the object that evolves (Figure 1). This separation makes the learned knowledge inspectable, but it also exposes a generalization question. A policy can improve its evolution score by accumulating broadly useful procedures or by fitting recipes to a few familiar tasks. Better training-suite performance alone does not distinguish the two. Nor does a growing code library show whether an agent still needs to adapt during a new run. We therefore examine the content of the evolved policies, their transfer to unseen tasks and other LLMs, and the contribution of decisions made after the initial optimizer change. Our contributions are: • An explicit policy-evolution framework for optimizer agents. RSI-Opt adds cross-run policy evolution to the within-run optimizer-agent setting. Our experiments connect a coding agent to an editable optimizer interface, allowing it to monitor training dynamics and revise update rules during a run. fixed baseline prompt, and four example tasks, with attribution and implementation details in Section 4. The contribution is the evolving policy, outer search, and study of the resulting knowledge. • An evaluation of transfer and online adaptation. We evaluate nine single-GPU tasks with three in-run LLMs, fresh evaluation seeds, comparisons of reported means, and controls using an unedited library template, a frozen first optimizer change, a one-decision agent, and the full agent. Three tasks guide evolution; three ML tasks and three PDE problems test transfer beyond that suite. • Evidence of selective transfer and specialization. Evolved policies improve the training suite for all three LLMs. GPT-5.5 and GPT-6.1 improve the mean summary score in every task group; Opus 5.5 improves on four of six held-out tasks but has a lower aggregate held-out summary score. Initial adaptation captures most of the observed benefit on seen tasks, while later decisions improve unseen-task performance for both baseline and evolved agents. Held-out ML transfer peaks early as continued evolution increasingly fits the training suite.

papers.title: ConsMSA: Semantic Distribution Consistency Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to predict human sentiments by integrating signals from different modalities such as text, video, and audio. However, raw multimodal sequences often suffer from semantic inconsistency--exhibiting redundancy or conflicts within and across modalities--which hinders robust understanding and increases computational cost. To this end, we introduce ConsMSA, which explicitly formalizes semantic distribution consistency across both $\textit{intra}$- and $\textit{inter}$-modality, providing a consistency-aware mechanism for robust and efficient multimodal sentiment prediction. Specifically, ConsMSA projects multimodal token features into a shared sentiment space to compute an Intra- and Inter-modality Consistency Score ($I^2CS$). By coupling this score with predictive relevance, we formulate consistency-aware importance signals that are utilized: (i) as a consistency regularizer to align latent distributions during training, (ii) to derive semantic-aware weights for adaptive multimodal token reweighting, and (iii) as a practical criterion to prune redundant or conflicting tokens. Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS demonstrate that ConsMSA achieves state-of-the-art performance while remaining robust under aggressive token compression--retaining only 10% of tokens yields comparable accuracy. These results establish semantic distribution consistency as a promising foundation for synergizing predictive robustness with computational efficiency.

papers.intro:
Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) aims to infer human sentiments by integrating heterogeneous signals such as spoken language, facial expression, and vocal prosody (Geetha et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2022a). Modern MSA systems, especially Transformer-based, typically encode each modality into token-level representations and rely on cross-modal interaction mechanisms, such as cross-attention, to aggregate cues across time and modalities (Wu et al., 2024). Despite strong empirical progress, a persistent bottleneck remains: token-level evidence is often semantically inconsistent. This occurs intra-modality due to pervasive redundancy or neutral signals, and inter-modality due to semantic conflicts, such as those found in sarcasm. papers.title: Does LeWorldModel Preserve Local Action Geometry?
papers.abstract: We examine how closely pretrained LeWorldModel (LeWM) reproduces the effects of small action changes. Using matched simulator and model responses, we measure action sensitivity with Gram matrices at three perturbation scales. Across nearly a thousand states from Reacher and OGBench Cube, the most sensitive action directions differ by median angles of about $36^\circ$ and $42^\circ$, respectively, at the smallest scale. Increasing the perturbation tenfold reduces median normalized Gram discrepancy by roughly 70\% on Reacher and 47\% on Cube. Geometry measured in pixels and embeddings varies more across scales than the chosen physical-state geometry. On held-out directions, environment Grams achieve median embedding response errors of 17\% and 28\%, compared with 26\% and 38\% for an isotropic reference with the same trace. LeWM's errors are higher at this scale. These findings support scale-specific evaluation of action sensitivity; its effect on control remains an open question.

Accurate prediction at a sampled action does not establish that nearby action directions have the correct relative effects. This motivates evaluating action sensitivity alongside aggregate prediction and control scores.

papers.title: HyScale: Scaling Long-Context Training for Learned Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: We present HyScale, a long-context training system for learned sparse attention. Learned sparse attention is a promising architecture for million-token contexts, widely adopted in production since DeepSeek-V3.2. Selection, however, grows into the training bottleneck. For each query, it scores every previous token whereas sparse attention reads only $k$; worse, current systems materialize a full score table and repeat selection during recomputation. Our key insight is that the output of selection is not an activation, but rather a set of indices. Building on it, HyScale introduces HyTopK and selection replay. HyTopK finds each query's exact top-$k$ on the fly without a score table, while selection replay reuses forward-pass selection in recomputation. Together with holistic system optimizations tackling end-to-end training challenges, HyScale speeds up GLM-5.1 training on 1M-token sequences by 2.07$\times$ over Megatron-LM on 512 H20 GPUs. It also speeds up the CSA layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and the QSA layers of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by 2.01$\times$ and 1.57$\times$ at 1M tokens on 32 H800 GPUs.

At these lengths, full attention dominates training cost: its computation grows quadratically with context length because each query attends to every previous token.

Learned sparse attention (Yuan et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) reduces this cost by splitting attention into two steps. In selection, a lightweight indexer scores every previous token for each query and keeps the top-kk. In sparse attention, each query attends only to the selected tokens. Token-level designs, pioneered by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), are widely adopted in production models such as GLM-5.1 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026) and Hy4 preview (Tencent-Hunyuan, 2026). Realizing this insight in end-to-end training raises three challenges. First, on-the-fly top-kk selection must decide whether to retain or discard each score immediately upon computation. Existing sampling-based top-kk operators (Yin et al., 2026) estimate a score threshold for inference, but break down in training: sampling is incompatible with context parallelism (CP), threshold under-estimation overflows fixed buffers, and selection becomes non-deterministic. Second, existing selective recomputation policies (Korthikanti et al., 2023; PyTorch, 2026) operate at the granularity of whole operators, whereas the indexer loss requires only the kk selected scores. Consequently, recomputation must either retain the full score table or rescore all previous tokens merely to recover kk values per query. Third, once selection is accelerated, CP communication and inefficient sparse kernels become exposed. papers.title: The Path to NDE 4.0: A Review of Algorithms, Techniques, and Strategies for Autonomous Inspection
papers.abstract: Non-Destructive Inspection (NDI) is a cornerstone of modern quality assurance, critical for ensuring the safety and reliability of infrastructure and manufactured components without causing damage. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the current NDI landscape, analyzing the field through four distinct lenses, namely, computational algorithms, physical techniques, industrial applications, and research objectives. We synthesize a broad range of academic literature to illustrate the rapid evolution from manual, analog interpretation to a digitized, data-centric paradigm known as NDE 4.0. Our analysis highlights the dominance of ultrasound and visual inspection as primary physical techniques, while revealing a significant shift toward deep learning and generative models for automated defect recognition. Despite these technological strides, the industry faces critical bottlenecks, notably the scarcity of standardized open-access datasets and the "black box" nature of AI models, which hinders widespread adoption. By charting these developments and identifying key research gaps, such as the need for explainable AI (XAI) and standardized digital twin protocols, this review offers a strategic roadmap for future research. It concludes that the future of NDI research should focus on the successful integration of intelligent, autonomous fusion of inspection data with advanced sensor technologies into asset lifecycle management.
papers.intro:
The process of non-destructive inspection (NDI) is an integral component of modern manufacturing and quality assurance, though its origins extend back for centuries. While its simplest form, direct visual inspection, is a practice as old as manufacturing itself, the Industrial Revolution and the technological advancements that followed spurred the rapid evolution and automation of NDI techniques. Consequently, a vast body of research has emerged to standardize, improve, and perfect NDI processes across diverse industries [61, 15, 32, 20, 26]. This field is currently undergoing a fundamental transformation. Historically characterized by manual data interpretation and analog measurement techniques [1, 46], the discipline is rapidly migrating toward a digitized, automated, and data-centric paradigm often termed NDE 4.0 [49]. This shift is driven by the convergence of advanced sensor physics, high-performance computing, and artificial intelligence. Recent academic literatures reflect this transition intensely, revealing a landscape where the boundaries between physical inspection and computational modeling are becoming increasingly blurred.

The Algorithms category investigates computational methods designed to automate the NDI process. The Techniques category encompasses literature regarding the physical technologies and methodologies applied during inspection. Papers within the Application Areas category examine NDI applications and the current technological standards across various industrial sectors. Finally, the Research Type category groups studies according to their primary research objectives. This structured classification highlights both the established strengths and the ongoing challenges within NDI research. papers.title: End-to-End Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning for Physics-Informed Optimization
papers.abstract: Optimizing high-dimensional physical systems under expensive evaluations and complex constraints is a central challenge in science and engineering. In offline model-based optimization (MBO), methods must improve designs using only a fixed dataset and no test-time access to the true objective. However, existing methods typically suffer from conservatism, unconstrained surrogate exploitation, or function as static inference-time samplers that cannot refine candidates against precise physical objectives. In this paper, we propose Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning (D2C) for offline MBO, which leverages the fact that deterministic sampling makes the reverse denoising chain differentiable with respect to the conditioning signal. D2C turns a frozen conditional diffusion model into an end-to-end gradient-based optimizer by directly optimizing conditioning variables at test time via gradients from frozen surrogate objectives and physics-informed penalties backpropagated through the reverse chain. We implement this idea in a composed proposer-evaluator framework and evaluate it on laser pulse optimization for inertial confinement fusion, sustainable data-center workload scheduling, and four Design-Bench tasks. Our method achieves the strongest results on the two real-world tasks and the best average rank across four Design-Bench tasks.
papers.intro:
The optimization of complex physical systems remains one of the most consequential challenges in science and engineering. Problems such as laser pulse shaping for inertial confinement fusion (ICF) and workload scheduling in large-scale data centers share a common structure: objective functions are computationally expensive to evaluate, the design space is high-dimensional with non-linear correlations, and candidate solutions must satisfy strict physical constraints where any violation carries safety-critical consequences.

The optimization of complex physical systems remains one of the most consequential challenges in science and engineering. Problems such as laser pulse shaping for inertial confinement fusion (ICF) and workload scheduling in large-scale data centers share a common structure: objective functions are computationally expensive to evaluate, the design space is high-dimensional with non-linear correlations, and candidate solutions must satisfy strict physical constraints where any violation carries safety-critical consequences.

The offline model-based optimization (MBO) paradigm addresses the evaluation-cost bottleneck by learning entirely from a fixed dataset of previously evaluated designs, with no access to the true objective at test time. Within this paradigm, existing approaches fall into three broad families. Forward (surrogate-based) methods train a neural network to approximate the objective and perform gradient ascent in design space [31, 9]; while effective, optimizing directly in unconstrained design space can move into regions poorly supported by the offline data, where the surrogate is unreliable. Inverse methods learn a conditional mapping from target performance labels to designs [2, 19, 18, 22]; these tend to stay closer to the empirical data distribution but are limited by the performance ceiling of the training labels and struggle to extrapolate beyond observed optima. Trajectory-based methods construct synthetic improvement paths and train generative models to imitate optimization dynamics [3, 39]; while powerful, they remain inference-time samplers whose conditioning targets are fixed prior to generation, with no mechanism to refine designs against downstream objectives.

A common limitation across these families is the lack of a direct, differentiable path from a physics-informed objective back to the generative process. The conditioning signal that steers generation is treated as a static input rather than an optimizable variable. This decoupling is especially limiting in safety-critical physical domains where the objective is not a single scalar score but a composite of performance metrics, conservation laws, and hard feasibility constraints that must be jointly satisfied.

papers.title: Permission to Retry: A Study of Authorization and Recovery in AI Agent Workflows
papers.abstract: A durable agent can resume a consequential action while its authority changes and the action's external outcome remains uncertain. We study execution-time reliability of tool-using AI agents, isolating recovery decisions from language-model behavior. Checkpoint state, permission to dispatch, evidence of an external effect and permission to reconcile are distinct obligations. We present a finite conformance study that checks these obligations through histories scored against a provider effect ledger hidden from the recovering application. A prospectively frozen campaign executes 336 histories on native LangGraph and Temporal hosts, crossing 14 schedules, three provider contracts and four matched application policies. All 168 paired host cells have identical checked outcomes. Per host, retained-ledger reconciliation passes all 42 histories: 21 checked completions, 15 denials and six unknown outcomes with reservations retained. Cached retry, revalidation before retry and stable-key retry pass 30, 36 and 31 histories respectively. A separate 16-case component study of InfinityOS, an enterprise AI platform developed by Arya.ai, exercises exported authority, worker, recovery and settlement code over repository fakes. The results isolate the roles of current authority, provider contracts and retained observations in recovery, with safety, completion and unresolved obligations reported separately for the declared application profile.
papers.intro:
Consider a refund for an approved recipient and amount. The service commits the refund, but the acknowledgement disappears. Before a replacement worker resumes, the initiating principal loses write permission. Repeating the request can create a duplicate; treating a missing acknowledgement as proof of failure can release an obligation prematurely; abandoning every continuation can prevent legitimate recovery. Recovering evidence of an existing effect and obtaining authority for a new dispatch are separate decisions.

papers.title: Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?
papers.abstract: Distilling interactive LLM agents requires choosing between teacher-generated demonstrations and student-generated experience, corresponding broadly to off-policy and on-policy distillation. While both have proven effective, we argue that this distinction is inherently hierarchical: the policy that induces an interaction history need not be the same as the policy that generates the token prefix of the current action. We introduce a hierarchical agent distillation framework that formalizes these two levels of on-policiness and enables explicit control over their pairing, mixture proportions, and training schedule. We study this problem through self-distillation, where a frozen teacher has access to task guidance unavailable to the student, and conduct a three-stage controlled study across three models and four interactive environments. We find that student-induced histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone training signal, whereas following the student at both levels generally performs worst. Nevertheless, fully on-policy data becomes beneficial when incorporated into a mixture with other configurations. Moreover, mixtures with identical teacher/student proportions at each level can yield substantially different performance, showing that how the two levels are paired matters beyond the overall amount of on-policy data. Finally, front-loading fully teacher-generated contexts and delaying fully on-policy contexts improves over a static mixture. These findings provide practical principles for deciding where, how much, and when agent distillation should follow the student.

Off-policy approaches train on teacher-generated trajectories (Kang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b), providing coherent demonstrations but limited exposure to states encountered by the student. An agent’s training context contains two nested levels. At the history level, preceding interactions determine the context and environment state before the current action. For example, a teacher can generate an action from a student-induced history, while a student can generate an action from a teacher-induced history. The relevant question is therefore not only whether training is on-policy, but at which level and to what extent should distillation follow the student?

papers.title: Agreement rather than normalisation keeps depth reusable in looped language models
papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one block of layers repeatedly, and the design pays off only if depth is reusable: loop steps beyond the trained budget must remain usable at inference. We ask whether that rests on normalising the state between loop steps, as the released Ouro models do, or on agreement between the loop a model is trained with and the loop it is run with. On released weights this loop-boundary normalisation can be removed without adding parameters and with the readout path bit-identical, and the operation is an identity at one loop step, which serves as an implementation check. Removing it takes Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B to zero accuracy by the trained budget on a balanced binary task (chance 0.500). State-norm growth, the failure that prior accounts predict, is not the cause: the norm stays within a factor of 2.021 while the head commits to a single wrong token. Yet in 19M-parameter models trained from scratch on two synthetic tasks, 16 seeds per configuration, training without the normalisation is never worse than training with it and extrapolates better: the two are closest at the trained depth and separate on both sides of it (Cliff's delta up to 0.867 beyond the budget). Both results follow if agreement, and not the normalisation itself, is what keeps depth reusable. The damage sits in the readout together with the last layer of the block: in the models trained from scratch, refitting the head over the frozen modified loop recovers a third of the lost accuracy and plateaus, while refitting the last block layer with it recovers all of it. Finally, comparing looped with stacked depth at an equal inference loop count is confounded by unequal overshoot of the trained budget; at matched overshoot the advantage of looping vanishes on one task and shrinks on the other.

papers.title: Sharp Bounds on the Winner's Bias under Independent and Nonnegatively Correlated Noise
papers.abstract: Reporting the best of $M$ noisy, unbiased scores overstates the winner's value by up to $c\sqrt{V}$, where $V$ is the total noise variance and the sharp constant $c$ depends on how the noise is dependent. It was known only at the two extremes, arbitrary dependence ($\sqrt{(M-1)/M}$) and i.i.d. noise. We determine it for two classes in between: for independent, not identically distributed noise it is $\sqrt{(M-1)/(2M)}$, and for pairwise nonnegatively correlated noise it is $(M-1)/M$; for uncorrelated noise this answers the maximum version of an open question about the expected range. Explicit finite constructions attain both. As a corollary, the bias of the cross-validation estimator is bounded sharply within each class. All theorems are formally verified in Lean 4. Across 448 language-model and classifier selection pipelines, designs with per-candidate items realize a median 0.75 of the independent-class ceiling. At a fixed item budget, scoring all candidates on shared items is markedly less optimistic than giving each candidate its own items.

Every theorem, corollary and lemma in the paper is machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, in about 7,900 lines with no sorry and no axioms beyond Lean’s standard three. The statements are formalized for random variables on an arbitrary probability space, with independence, square integrability and zero mean as explicit hypotheses, so the formal theorems are those stated here and not special cases. Attainment and the suprema are formalized too, so sharpness is checked as well as the bounds. Appendix E maps each result to its Lean name. The formalization will be released together with the code and the score matrices of the numerical study.

papers.title: BARC-Bench: Benign Asks, Risky Consequences
papers.abstract: Task instructions from users for agents are inherently underspecified, especially regarding safety boundaries--creating behavioral risks. To study these risks, we introduce BARC-Bench, a collection of 110 tasks across nine simulated workspace environments where benign requests leave openings for unsafe actions. In this benchmark, we evaluate agent behavior against safety boundaries established by workspace records, implicit environmental context, and unstated social norms. For example, an agent asked to schedule off-boarding discussions must arrange the meeting without prematurely revealing an employee's resignation through a shared calendar invitation. Evaluating four frontier model configurations across five attempts per task reveals that models are not consistently safe: the share of tasks completed safely on all five attempts ranges from 9.1% to 72.7%, with even the strongest configuration producing a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks. These results highlight an asymmetric operational risk: while models frequently complete complex workflows, their inability to consistently respect unstated boundaries presents a substantial barrier to safe autonomous delegation.
papers.intro:
Routine workflow requests are often straightforward to execute but still require consequential judgment. For example, consider a manager who wants to schedule a meeting about an employee’s departure. The manager has to decide who the attendees are, the time, and what to put on the calendar invite title and description. If the departure is not yet public knowledge, then a descriptive calendar title in a shared calendar invite, as in common in most workplaces, would leak sensitive information. The meeting can be scheduled successfully while still causing workplace harm. As modern agents become increasingly more capable of executing these tasks, we want to examine how reliably they avoid such harms.

These tasks that require judgment over subtle workplace safety considerations are common in everyday work, spanning not just interpersonal relationships like the example above but also typical workplace activities such as handling files or managing records. To complicate agent judgment more, real-world, routine prompts and tasks are often flawed: under-specified, ambiguous, or written under the user’s incorrect or outdated assumptions [16, 19, 18, 8]. Unlike many other safety-oriented tasks, these requests are benign—they do not harbor any malicious intent or try to bypass security safeguards. However, the underlying safety boundaries may conflict with the requested action. Even if the action is allowed, decisions about the content or audience can make the action unsafe. The agent must determine how to complete the user’s goal without crossing any safety boundaries.

We study agents’ workplace safety under benign asks: whether agents can accomplish valid workplace requests without taking any harmful actions in the process. These judgments require careful assessment of the surrounding context. The same action, such as disclosing an appointment’s purpose or org-internal constraint, can be appropriate with some audiences but not others [12]. Relevant context may be distributed across different surfaces, including the prompt, messages within the environment, or workspace documents or tools. Assessing model quality on only whether it can produce the intended response or artifact to the prompt can miss consequential, harmful mistakes or side effects.

Existing evaluations study task completion and the ability to refuse harmful requests, defend against prompt injection, and comply with safety policies. We offer to complement prior work by examining the consequences of agent choices within realistic, routine workflows found in business and personal productivity operations. To this end, we introduce BARC-Bench (Benign Asks, Risky Consequences), a benchmark of 110 tasks across 9 simulated environments to study this setting. Tasks are grounded in documents, communication histories, and other artifacts available to an agent. The dataset is built with diverse environments generated with AI assistance, human-authored and curated seed tasks, and AI-assisted task expansion using the seeds.

papers.title: CEMIR vs. FISER: a comparative study of reasoning-based and enrichment-based approaches to pragmatic intent recognition
papers.abstract: Intent recognition in human-robot interaction requires agents to resolve ambiguous natural language instructions by inferring the speaker's underlying goals. Research has increasingly focused on two notable paradigms for addressing this task: structured symbolic reasoning and multimodal input enrichment. However, it remains unclear whether enrichment-based methods provide benefit in settings where the ambiguity concerns unstated human intent rather than missing observable scene information. In this paper, we present a comparative and diagnostic study benchmarking FISER - a framework utilizing structured social and embodied reasoning - against CEMIR (Context-Enriched Multimodal Intent Recognition), a method that performs multimodal enrichment by synthesizing narratives and photorealistic images from textual prompts. By evaluating both approaches across four Large Language Models (LLMs), ranging from Qwen2.5-Omni-3B to GPT-5, on the HandMeThat v2 benchmark, we analyze their capability to resolve pragmatic ambiguities. Our statistical analysis, employing multiple-comparison correction, reveals no statistically significant difference in performance between FISER and CEMIR across any model or difficulty level. This pattern holds across all sixteen model-by-difficulty comparisons, as well as in a targeted ablation isolating CEMIR's narrative and visual components. Instead, performance is primarily associated with backbone capability and the inherent difficulty of the ambiguity. These findings suggest a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment: when the relevant task constraints are already available in the textual instruction, synthetic multimodal augmentation may not provide measurable benefit over structured reasoning on the same text.

authors.name: Ziya Hosseynzadeh
authors.institution: Iran University of Science and Technology

papers.intro:
Interactive AI systems such as smart home assistants, service robots, and virtual chatbots must infer user intent to act reliably and safely in everyday environments [1]. Intent recognition, the task of identifying the goal behind a user’s instruction or action, is therefore a foundational component of natural language understanding in interactive settings, where misinterpretations can cause incorrect actions, breakdowns in collaboration, or degraded user trust [2, 3, 4]. In domestic and assistive scenarios, users frequently omit details and rely on shared context, routines, and unspoken goals [5]; consequently, brief utterances such as ”Could you pass that?” can be under-specified without additional grounding [6]. As communicative ambiguity increases, maintaining fluent and dependable human-AI/robot collaboration requires mechanisms that connect what is said to what is meant, and ultimately to what should be done [7]. Meeting this requirement raises a basic design question that recurs across language understanding tasks more broadly: where should a system look to resolve what remains unclear? Prior work differs in its answer. One line of work treats the missing information as already recoverable from what is given to the agent, the human’s prior actions and the language of the instruction itself, and resolves ambiguity through explicit, structured reasoning over that input; FISER [8] exemplifies this approach on the HandMeThat benchmark [9], decomposing intent recognition into a social reasoning stage and an embodied reasoning stage, and demonstrating strong performance using purely textual episode representations. A second line of work instead enriches the model’s input with additional context before reasoning takes place, whether directly observed from the environment or, more recently, generated from the text itself, and has an established record of small but consistent gains on other language understanding tasks such as classification and QA [10, 11, 12, 13]. These two lines of work have developed largely independently and have not been evaluated under conditions the other is built for: reasoning-based approaches have been tested on tasks like HandMeThat [9] where ambiguity is pragmatic, the environment is fully described, and what remains uncertain is the human’s intent, while enrichment-based approaches have been tested only on tasks where the missing information is a directly observable property of a static scene, or on single-step classification and QA judgments (Research Gap section). HandMeThat v2 offers a setting where this comparison becomes possible, and one where a strong reasoning-based baseline, FISER, already exists. The benchmark’s textual interface deliberately withholds nothing perceptual: every object and its relevant properties are already stated in the episode text; this also means that any additional signal supplied to the model can only be self-generated, not genuinely external to the text, isolating the specific form of enrichment this study investigates from perceptual grounding based on direct observation. The present study investigates whether an enrichment-based alternative can match or exceed FISER under this kind of ambiguity. We introduce CEMIR (Context-Enriched Multimodal Intent Recognition), which augments each action step of a HandMeThat v2 episode with a generated narrative and a corresponding generated image, produced entirely from the episode text rather than from any independent observation of the environment. The decision to combine narrative and visual elaboration jointly, rather than testing either in isolation, is motivated by Winston’s Strong Story and Directed Perception Hypotheses, which hold that narrative plays a central role in human intelligence, and that much of human commonsense is derived by deploying perceptual apparatus on real and imagined events [14]; we adopt this as a design rationale for CEMIR’s approach to resolving referential ambiguity, not as a claim on Winston’s part about generated modalities or ambiguity resolution specifically. We evaluate CEMIR against FISER on 400 episodes from HandMeThat v2, across four language models ranging from 3B to GPT-5 scale, using a cluster-level paired permutation test with Holm–Bonferroni correction applied within each family of comparisons. Because CEMIR and FISER differ in both prompting structure and input modality, each is evaluated as a complete system representing its own paradigm; Ablation Study section separately reports how CEMIR’s own performance changes when its narrative or image component is removed, to characterize their individual contributions within CEMIR’s architecture. This work makes two contributions. First, we introduce CEMIR, an enrichment-based alternative to structured text-only reasoning for object and goal identification under pragmatic ambiguity. Second, we provide an empirical comparison between FISER and CEMIR across model scales and difficulty levels, together with a within-system ablation of CEMIR’s narrative and visual components, addressing a comparison that, to our knowledge, existing work on synthetic multimodal augmentation has not examined.

papers.title: Topological Equivalence of Spectral and Density Cluster Hierarchies
papers.abstract: We compare two canonical ways to recover hierarchical clustering from an underlying density $f$: the \emph{density cluster tree} given by connected components of superlevel sets $\{f\ge\lambda\}$, and a \emph{spectral hierarchy} obtained by applying single linkage to diffusion distances induced by a Laplacian operator. We give conditions under which, at an appropriate diffusion time, the diffusion hierarchy is \emph{topologically equivalent} to the density cluster tree up to a monotone rescaling of heights. It further shows that a $k$-NN graph implementation inherits this equivalence from uniform approximation of diffusion distances, yielding a finite-sample reduction from spectral graph constructions to density-level-set topology.
papers.intro:
Hierarchical clustering is a basic tool to describe structure in data at many scales. In this paper we study two standard hierarchies that start from an unknown density ff on a compact domain MM. The first one is the density cluster tree TfT_{f}, defined by the connected components of the superlevel sets of the underlying density function Lλ={x∈M:f⁡(x)≥λ}L_{\lambda}=\{x\in M:f(x)\geq\lambda\} as λ\lambda decreases [7, 1, 5]. The second one is a diffusion–spectral hierarchy, defined as a reversible Markov operator PP (or a Laplacian) from ff[3, 15]. Both viewpoints share the same idea and define a cluster as a set where the random walk mixes fast inside, but it escapes slowly outside.

Both viewpoints share the same idea and define a cluster as a set where the random walk mixes fast inside, but it escapes slowly outside.

The question we ask is simple. The density cluster tree is a canonical topological object, and it comes with a clear statistical target and stability theory [1, 5]. Diffusion distances are very popular because they are algorithmic and robust, and they are connected to spectral gaps and bottlenecks [3, 15]. But it is not always clear what the diffusion hierarchy estimates as a population object. So, when does the diffusion single-linkage hierarchy give the same merge structure as the density cluster tree? This allows to consider the spectral method more than a heuristic, considering it as a certified estimator of a topological object defined by ff.

papers.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
papers.abstract: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.

papers.title: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.
papers.intro:
MLLMs have recently been adopted for autonomous driving, where a single model takes raw sensor input and outputs both a textual rationale and a driving decision (Cui et al., 2024). This makes them a natural fit for tasks where the model must explain its choices, such as following natural-language navigation commands or justifying a lane change.

MLLMs have recently been adopted for autonomous driving, where a single model takes raw sensor input and outputs both a textual rationale and a driving decision (Cui et al., 2024). This makes them a natural fit for tasks where the model must explain its choices, such as following natural-language navigation commands or justifying a lane change.

However, driving differs from one-shot question-answering tasks. The agent observes the scene only partially, and the scene keeps changing as it moves. Traffic is also full of ambiguity. For example, a slowing vehicle may be yielding, preparing to turn, or reacting to an unseen obstacle; a pedestrian near the curb may intend to cross or remain waiting. In these cases, multiple explanations can remain plausible at the same time. Several existing MLLM-based driving systems generate a single rationale or planned trajectory at each inference step (Xu et al., 2024; Mao et al., 2023; Renz et al., 2025). This single-chain reasoning is fluent but brittle: the model picks one interpretation too early, then has to act on it whether or not later frames support it. Figure 1 contrasts the two paradigms: a single chain of thought per frame, versus a set of hypotheses that is carried forward and reweighted over time. This premature commitment is especially problematic in closed-loop control. Once the model forms a wrong interpretation, the resulting action may change subsequent observations in ways that reinforce the initial mistake. Existing uncertainty estimation methods for large language models (LLMs) mainly focus on output variability across multiple generations (Ye et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a). These methods are useful, but they measure uncertainty over multiple answers to the same question, not how uncertainty changes as new frames arrive. To address this limitation, we propose DriveMind, a closed-loop driving framework that maintains a time-evolving belief state over multiple reasoning hypotheses. DriveMind represents the agent’s reasoning state as a weighted set of natural-language hypotheses. Each hypothesis describes a possible interpretation of the scene, and its weight represents its relative support under the accumulated observations. As new frames arrive, DriveMind updates the hypotheses themselves and reweights them based on the new evidence. For real-time closed-loop control, DriveMind adopts an asynchronous fast-slow Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture. The slow subsystem uses an MLLM to perform multi-hypothesis reasoning and belief tracking. The fast subsystem runs at control frequency and uses a diffusion-based controller to generate waypoint trajectories conditioned on the latest belief. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking improves DS from 68.50 to 81.37 and SR from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur in scenarios requiring intent disambiguation, such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS). On NAVSIM, belief tracking improves PDMS from 78.2 to 81.0. Ablations support the effectiveness of belief tracking, while runtime analysis demonstrates the efficiency of asynchronous inference. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce DriveMind, a closed-loop driving framework that maintains a weighted set of natural-language hypotheses and updates them as new observations arrive. • We design an asynchronous fast-slow VLA architecture where a slow MLLM reasoner performs belief tracking and a fast diffusion controller generates real-time trajectories. • We show on Bench2Drive and NavSim that explicit belief tracking improves driving performance and robustness, with the largest gains on long-tail scenarios requiring intent disambiguation.

papers.title: TACS-RF: Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave Modules
papers.abstract: We present the framework of TACS-RF - a Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules. In this framework, a large-language-model (LLM) coding agent (Claude Opus 4.8) directly drives industry-standard electronic-design-automation (EDA) tools such as Cadence Virtuoso/Spectre, Calibre, Cadence EMX, and Ansys HFSS to design RF and mmWave modules. We validate the framework through the agentic design of a 240-251 GHz sub-THz transmitter in a 90 nm SiGe BiCMOS process. The agent semi-autonomously designed the sub-blocks including a 60 GHz push-push Colpitts VCO with second-harmonic extraction, multistage differential cascode power drivers, a push-push frequency doubler, a differential bowtie antenna, and all the interstage matching networks. The transmitter chain with parasitic-extracted devices and EM-verified passives delivers +5.1 to +6.3 dBm across an 11 GHz varactor-only tuning range, phase noise of -80 to -88 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset while consuming a DC power of 361 mW. We describe the agent-driven design flow and the resulting division of labor between human and agent, taking a step toward a "text-to-ASIC" future for designing RF/mmWave hardware.

papers.intro:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly reshaped how humans interact with information, and is increasingly expected to reshape scientific and engineering practice. In radio-frequency (RF) and millimeter-wave/sub-terahertz integrated circuit design specifically, algorithmic and AI-assisted approaches such as deep-learning-enabled inverse design of multi-port passives and integrated circuits [1] and pixelated, multilayered topology-optimization frameworks for millimeter-wave power amplifiers [2] have demonstrated that design automation can compress schematic and layout iteration cycles from weeks to days, while achieving state-of-the-art performance without hand-crafted templates. However, these methods are fundamentally contextless, requiring each new design target requires the underlying optimization to be re-run largely from scratch, without carrying forward circuit-design reasoning, prior topology knowledge, or engineering heuristics from prior work.

However, these methods are fundamentally contextless, requiring each new design target requires the underlying optimization to be re-run largely from scratch, without carrying forward circuit-design reasoning, prior topology knowledge, or engineering heuristics from prior work.

Large language models (LLMs), in contrast, are distinguished by their ability to reason over contextualized, cumulative knowledge such as retrieving relevant topologies, applying design equations, and adapting prior solutions to new specifications rather than re-discovering them numerically. Early studies have begun to demonstrate this potential for analog/mixed-signal design. Ref. [3] used multiple agent frameworks to automate operational-amplifier and analog-to-digital-converter netlist generation from natural-language specifications, decomposing the design task across specialized agents for topology selection, parameter extraction, and SPICE-level verification. Separately, LLM-based sizing agents integrated in a closed loop with circuit simulators have been shown to iteratively converge the design on analog OTA and digital gates [4]. However, they do not address the EM- and parasitic-aware co-design that dominates design closure at RF, mmWave and sub-THz frequencies.

In this work, we present TACS-RF: Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules, an LLM-agent-driven framework that accelerates the RF/mmWave/sub-THz module design with contextual awareness from prior publications [5, 6], while interacting with industry-standard tools (see Fig. 1). The tasks performed by the TACS framework include: (i) schematic generation and optimization, (ii) passives/antenna layout generation and EM simulations, (iii) transistor layout and parasitic extraction, (iv) reliability and final checks. These software tools used in the workflow are directly controlled by the agent through terminal with no human-GUI interfacing. The design prototype validating the TACS framework is a sub-THz (240–251 GHz) transmitter achieving a peak output power of +5.1 to +6.3 dBm and phase noise ≤\leq −-85 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset across the 6 GHz VCO tuning range. Through TACS-RF, design time and human labor can be reduced from months to a few days. Beyond this manuscript, we envision a “text-to-ASIC” future where RF/mmWave circuit design, layout, and optimization tasks are reduced to prompt engineering and simulation verification.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Curriculum Learning Depends on Reward Sparsity and Competing Optima
papers.abstract: While animals and people tend to learn a task more quickly and reliably when they first train on simpler versions of it, curriculum learning's effectiveness in artificial settings varies, and appears substantially greater in reinforcement learning than in supervised learning. In this work, we construct and analyze a minimal model of policy learning to better understand why. We consider an open-loop, episodic target interception task whose parameters---especially how close the agent must be to the target to receive an informative reward signal---can be chosen so that the agent either receives informative rewards frequently ('dense' rewards) or rarely ('sparse' rewards). We mathematically and numerically analyze the dynamics of REINFORCE-based policy learning in both cases. In the dense reward case, curricula have only marginal benefits; in the sparse case, curricula can be required for learning to occur at all. We find that this is especially true when the agent has the conflicting goals of minimizing effort and accumulating high reward, since this can produce distinct reward landscape optima which compete with one another. Our characterization of useful curricula in this setting indicates that they address two issues: they (i) make rewards less sparse to speed up learning, and (ii) shape the reward landscape to steer agents away from bad local optima.

Animals and humans typically require a structured progression to acquire complex skills [26]. But in machine learning, curriculum learning (CL) [3, 33] is not universally useful. In supervised settings CL often yields little improvement [35, 11], whereas it can be highly effective in reinforcement learning (RL) [28] if task difficulty gradually increases [20, 23, 14]. Compounding this puzzle, the few existing analytical studies predict at best modest effects [24, 18]. Why might curricula be essential for biological learners, but not necessarily for artificial learners?

In supervised settings CL often yields little improvement [35, 11], whereas it can be highly effective in reinforcement learning (RL) [28] if task difficulty gradually increases [20, 23, 14]. Compounding this puzzle, the few existing analytical studies predict at best modest effects [24, 18]. Why might curricula be essential for biological learners, but not necessarily for artificial learners?

One major difference between supervised learning and RL is reward sparsity: learners may receive informative rewards only rarely, because they require highly specific actions or action sequences [17]. Our first hypothesis is that reward sparsity greatly impacts the effectiveness of CL, because adapting task difficulty to the agent’s ability can effectively de-sparsify rewards [8, 2, 6]. A second (not unrelated) major difference is that multiple locally optimal strategies are more likely to coexist, and learned strategies may strongly depend on initialization and learning dynamics [13, 1]. Our second hypothesis is that competing optima greatly impact the effectiveness of CL, because CL can shape loss landscapes to steer agents away from bad (i.e., not reward-maximizing) optima.

In this work, our goal is to better understand the effectiveness of CL by studying a minimal model of policy learning. Our setting is simple enough to analyze mathematically, but possesses qualitative features critical to answering our question, including (i) reward sparsity, and (ii) competing optima. The structure of the task we study mimics target interception problems, where an agent must learn to intercept a small target; a primary difficulty is that the agent may not receive an informative reward unless they reach the target, which initially happens rarely. Our main contributions are: • We introduce a tractable model of policy learning given a sparse, multimodal return. • We show that reward sparsity can produce exponentially slow learning without curricula. • We show that competing optima can produce ‘quitting’ without curricula. • We show useful curricula address these issues. Finally, in Sec. 5 we characterize useful curricula, and show that they effectively de-sparsify rewards and steer agents away from bad optima.

papers.title: Scaling Transformer Energy-based Models For High Quality Image Synthesis
papers.abstract: Energy-Based Models (EBMs) are a flexible class of generative models that decouple probabilistic modeling from the generation process. This decoupling directly enables compositional generation and inference-time scaling, where sample quality can be refined simply by increasing sampling steps. However, severe challenges in high-dimensional sampling and training instabilities with deep architectures have restricted EBMs to low-dimensional regimes. To resolve these bottlenecks, we introduce the Transformer Energy-Based Model (TEM), a scalable transformer energy function operating entirely within a latent space. On top of this backbone, we extract energies at multiple layers and sum them, composing complementary constraints from local texture to global semantics. Furthermore, two components make this high-quality at scale: Positive Representation Alignment (PRA), which supervises TEM's intermediate representations with a vision foundation model, and advanced sampling strategies that improve sample quality at inference. TEM-XL achieves an FID-50K of 3.82 on class-conditional ImageNet 256$\times$256 without classifier-free guidance, showing that a contrastive EBM can generate high-fidelity images. On ImageNet 512$\times$512, TEM achieves an FID-50K of 8.24, demonstrating that the approach scales to higher resolution. We further validate the core promises of EBMs: compositional generation, zero-shot inpainting, and out-of-distribution detection.
papers.intro:
Energy-Based Models (EBMs) [23, 11] parameterize probability distributions via an energy function that assigns lower energies to more probable samples and higher energies to less probable samples. EBMs provide a flexible and mathematically elegant framework that fundamentally separates explicit generation from probabilistic modeling. Unlike Diffusion [18, 38] and Flow [24] models, which are mathematically constrained to pre-defined generative trajectories governed by carefully designed timestep schedules, EBMs define the data distribution solely through an energy function, entirely decoupling the model from the generative process. This decoupling of the model from the generative process yields profound advantages. First, EBMs decouple learning from inference, allowing the sampling procedure to be chosen independently of model training. This enables flexible test-time compute scaling by increasing the MCMC steps, progressively refining the samples through a deeper exploration of the learned energy landscape. Second, this flexibility enables the composition of different distributions together [11, 9], which can enable zero-shot generation and generalization capabilities.

This decoupling of the model from the generative process yields profound advantages. First, EBMs decouple learning from inference, allowing the sampling procedure to be chosen independently of model training. This enables flexible test-time compute scaling by increasing the MCMC steps, progressively refining the samples through a deeper exploration of the learned energy landscape. Second, this flexibility enables the composition of different distributions together [11, 9], which can enable zero-shot generation and generalization capabilities.

However, despite their theoretical advantages and compositional properties, EBMs have struggled with widespread adoption due to several critical unresolved challenges. First, EBMs face severe vulnerability to the curse of dimensionality: MCMC sampling suffers from poor mixing in high-dimensional spaces, leading to slow convergence and mode collapse. Second, EBMs scale poorly with model capacity. As network depth increases, conventional architectures exhibit severe training instability, making robust optimization exceedingly difficult [11, 10]. Consequently, existing EBM research has been largely limited to smaller-scale benchmarks, unable to demonstrate competitive performance on challenging, high-resolution datasets.

papers.title: Controlled Evaluation of EEG Foundation Models: Random Initialisation, Band-Power and Validation-Selected Probes
papers.abstract: EEG foundation models report downstream gains, yet their protocols seldom include three controls. These are the same encoder untrained, spectral features fitted on the same data, and a layer picked without looking at test scores. We therefore evaluate five publicly released EEG foundation models and an in-house JEPA-style model under one protocol with all three controls and several seeds, on five benchmarks and four added task families. The controls change the reading in three ways. First, picking the probed layer by its test score raises the layer-wise peak by an average of +0.034 and reverses the peak-versus-output gap in 9 of 36 cells. Second, with the layer picked on validation, random initialisation matches or beats pretraining for half of the models on sleep and emotion, and no model beats a five-band log-power baseline on emotion or motor imagery. Third, after full fine-tuning only 5 of 30 pairs gain beyond twice their seed spread, and the one clear loss of -0.290 AUROC persists under matched learning rates. From these results we draw four reporting practices, and we release every cell for re-analysis.

Recent EEG foundation models such as LaBraM (Jiang et al., 2024), EEGPT (Wang et al., 2024), CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025), LUNA (Döner et al., 2025) and LuMamba (Broustail et al., 2026) each report downstream gains under their own protocol, with its own splits, heads, schedules and hyperparameters. These protocols differ, so the published numbers cannot be compared across papers, and none of the papers evaluates the other models under its own protocol (Jiang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Döner et al., 2025). Three controls are missing from most of these reports. The three are a matched encoder of the same architecture at random initialisation, a band-power baseline on the same split, and a probed layer chosen on validation instead of on test (Section 3.4). Each is standard in representation-learning evaluation (Alain & Bengio, 2017; Musgrave et al., 2020; Pineau et al., 2018).

papers.title: Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust--Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in negotiations on behalf of individuals and organizations, yet they remain vulnerable to manipulation, particularly in repeated multi-party interactions. Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation models, whereas existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon. We investigate whether LLM agents can form useful trust estimates from prior interactions and leverage them to improve future negotiation outcomes. We introduce a repeated, multi-party, multi-issue negotiation framework in which recurring agents participate in a sequence of negotiation games while one participant covertly attempts to prevent agreement. After each game, agents assess their counterparts and maintain pairwise trust estimates that carry over to subsequent negotiations. We compare trust-aware and trust-agnostic agents and analyze how explicit trust influences negotiation outcomes. Our results reveal a \emph{trust--agreement gap}: trust-aware agents can identify the adversary within a few games, but accurate trust estimates do not consistently translate into better agreements. Trust increases agreement rates by up to 23 percentage points, but only when agents are explicitly guided to use it in their decisions. Explicit trust can therefore improve repeated LLM negotiations, but its value depends critically on how trust is assessed and incorporated into agents' reasoning.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) have evolved beyond chatbots that generate isolated responses. LLMs can interact with tools, combine reasoning with actions, and participate in complex multi-turn workflows. Multi-agent LLM systems extend these capabilities by enabling agents to communicate and coordinate as part of a larger decision-making process [45, 43]. As these systems mature, LLM agents will increasingly act on behalf of individuals and organizations [26, 29]. Emerging applications already employ LLMs in contract discussions and automated supplier negotiations [40]. Negotiation is therefore becoming a core capability for LLM agents: tasks such as allocating resources, negotiating contracts, and approving projects require prolonged deliberation among parties with different objectives [1]. To succeed in such settings, agents must remain robust when counterparts behave strategically or adversarially—for example, by using persuasion, concealing information, or attempting to manipulate the negotiation [30, 12].

We study this problem in multi-party scorable negotiation games [38], in which a group of organizations engages in repeated negotiations (Figure 1). In each game, a company proposes a project and negotiates its terms with a funding ministry, local communities, and advocacy groups. The parties deliberate over a set of issues, such as budget, location, and compensation, where each issue has several options, and a deal assigns one option to every issue. Every party privately scores the options according to its own priorities and accepts only deals that meet its minimum threshold. As the same parties meet again over new projects, each negotiation leaves behind evidence of who compromised, who obstructed, and who was reliable. Now suppose one participant covertly benefits if no agreement is reached: it can reject reasonable deals, push proposals others will oppose, and disguise obstruction as principled bargaining. A human negotiator in this situation would rely on trust built from past encounters to decide whose proposals to support and whose objections to discount. The central question we investigate is whether LLM agents can form and leverage such trust.

To investigate this question, we introduce TASMAN (Trust-Augmented Strategic Multi-Agent Negotiation), a repeated negotiation setting in which trust formed in one game informs the next. After each game, agents assess their counterparts with one of three methods: the beta reputation system (BRS) [20], where the LLM reports feedback and a Bayesian rule computes trust; rubric-based trust, where the LLM scores each counterpart on five predefined behavioral metrics; or free-form judgment, where the LLM chooses its own criteria. Agents carry these scores into the next game, with or without guidance on how to use them. We address four research questions: • RQ1—Trust formation: Can LLM agents form trust from negotiation history that distinguishes a covert adversary from cooperative counterparts, and how does this trust evolve over repeated negotiations? • RQ2—Trust assessment: Which assessment method produces more reliable trust: BRS adapted for LLMs, a predefined rubric, or the LLM’s own criteria? • RQ3—Negotiation outcomes: When does explicit trust improve negotiation outcomes, and how much of its value do agents leave unused (trust–agreement gap)? • RQ4—Agent reasoning: How does explicit trust change what agents reason about when they propose and vote?

papers.title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings where they pursue separate tasks while sharing resources and operating under review or oversight processes. Such settings create safety risks not only when agents are malicious, but also when they are simply trying to help. Prior work has largely studied adversarial or explicitly collusive behavior; we show that benign agents pursuing separate objectives can spontaneously cooperate in ways that bypass intended workflows. We call this the \emph{helpful agent problem}. We study long-horizon shared-resource environments in which agents sometimes depend on resources owned by their peers and cross-owner changes are normally mediated by a reviewer. When review becomes unavailable, agents begin making changes on one another's behalf despite having no shared reward or explicit incentive to cooperate. Crucially, these actions remain within each agent's local permissions while circumventing the system's intended oversight structure. We introduce \textsc{FavorBench}, a controlled benchmark with measurable downstream side effects, and adapt \textsc{CooperBench} to test the phenomenon in realistic repositories. Across two benchmarks and four models, we find that out-of-workflow favors emerge frequently. Further, in \textsc{FavorBench}, favors from at least three models cause significant harm to parties outside the interaction. These results reveal a distinct multi-agent safety challenge: cooperation itself can create pathways around system-level safeguards.

papers.title: Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring aims to detect potentially harmful behaviors in large language models (LLMs) from their CoTs. Intervention-based evaluations measure this property by asking whether a monitor can detect the role of an intervention from the CoT when the targeted behavior occurs, typically using minimal-criterion sensitivity ($\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$) proposed by~\citep{guan2025monitoring}. However, a target behavior observed under intervention is not necessarily caused by it, and we show that this metric can overestimate how often a monitor detects target behaviors actually caused by the intervention. Specifically, we establish $\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$ as an upper bound on this causal detection rate and derive a complementary lower bound, which provides a tighter evaluation framework for CoT monitorability. With this framework, we study whether LLMs can be trained to make their CoTs easier to monitor. We first construct a training dataset of paired control--intervention tasks spanning multiple intervention types. Using the dataset, we design and apply three intervention-specific training methods based on off-policy self-distillation, reinforcement learning, and on-policy self-distillation to train separate variants of each base model. Across various model-monitor configurations, all three methods generally improve CoT monitorability over the corresponding base models under our extended evaluation framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/xinyue-lxy/learning-to-be-monitored.

papers.intro:
The reasoning traces generated by large language models (LLMs) can provide clues about their final answers or actions. Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring uses these traces to infer properties of a model’s behavior, including reward hacking, deception, and reliance on particular information in the input. We use CoT monitorability to denote how reliably a monitor can infer the property of interest from the available reasoning trace, which depends on both the task model and the monitor setup (Guan et al., 2025). Typically, we focus on input-intervention monitorability: whether a monitor can detect evidence in a model’s CoT that a specified input intervention influenced its response. In agentic coding environments, access to CoT has enabled monitors to detect reward hacking more effectively than access to actions and outputs alone (Baker et al., 2025). These findings motivate CoT monitoring as an important safety measure (Korbak et al., 2025).

CoT monitoring depends on whether CoTs contain sufficient information about the behavior being monitored. However, models may fail to disclose factors that influence their decisions. For instance, biased prompts and hints can alter answers without being acknowledged in the reasoning (Turpin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025); optimization against CoT monitors can further encourage models to conceal reward hacking (Baker et al., 2025). Therefore, improving CoT monitorability requires enriching CoTs with decision-relevant information, rather than focusing solely on the monitor.
